en: The Amarakośa, titled Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana, Chapter 3:
the third section, the General Section (Sāmānyakāṇḍa).
Now begins the group of adjectives (Viśeṣyanighnavarga).

(3.0.1) By means of words that qualify a substantive, those that are synonymous, those with multiple meanings, and also indeclinables; (3.0.2) by means of collections concerning gender and so forth, the sections are based on general categories;
[this is] the technical terminology.
(3.0.3) Whatever is qualified by terms such as "woman" (*strī*) or "wife" (*dāra*), and by whatever kind of words that have been introduced,
(3.0.4) adjectives, nouns of substance, and nouns of action shall likewise be its qualifiers.
(3.1.5) The section on words subordinate to the qualified (*viśeṣyanighna*).

(3.1.6) He who brings security, he who grants safety, he who bestows auspiciousness, and he who creates welfare; (3.1.7) the doer of good deeds, the meritorious, the fortunate, and the noble-minded one who possesses great resolve;
(3.1.8) the kind-hearted, the benevolent, the one of great energy, and the one of great exertion.
(3.1.9) *Pravīṇa*, *nipuṇa*, *abhijña*, *vijña*, *niṣṇāta*, and *śikṣita* [mean one who is skilled];
(3.1.10) *vaijñānika*, *kṛtamukha*, *kṛtī*, and *kuśala* [also mean one who is skilled];
(3.1.11) *pūjya* and *pratīkṣya* [mean worthy of honor], while *sāṃśayika* refers to one whose mind is possessed by doubt.
(3.1.12) One who is worthy of gifts or deserving of an offering is called *dakṣiṇīya* or *dakṣiṇya*.
(3.1.13) A liberal man, one who is munificent, or one who is fond of giving, is called *vadānya*, *sthūlalakṣa*, or *dānaśauṇḍa*.
(3.1.14) One who is long-lived is *jaivātṛka* or *āyuṣmat*; one who knows the scriptures is *antarvāṇi*.
(3.1.15) A scrutinizer (*parīkṣaka*), one who reasons from causes (*kāraṇika*), and one who bestows boons (*varada*) is one who prospers (*samardhaka*).
(3.1.16) One who is gladdened (*harṣamāṇa*), one who undergoes transformation (*vikurvāṇa*), one whose mind is exalted (*pramanas*), and one whose mind is joyful (*hṛṣṭamānasa*).
(3.1.17) One who is dejected (*durmanas*), distracted (*vimanās*), inward-minded (*antarmanās*), longing (*utka*), and one whose mind is uplifted (*unmanās*).
(3.1.18) *dakṣiṇa* means straightforward and generous; *sukala* refers to one who is both a giver and an enjoyer.
(3.1.19) *tatpara*, *prasita*, and *āsakta* mean intent upon that; *utsuka* means one who is striving for a desired object.
(3.1.20) *pratīta*, *prathita*, *khyāta*, *vitta*, *vijñāta*, and *viśruta* all mean renowned or famous.
(3.1.21) But when [the meaning] is understood through qualities (*guṇa*), there are the terms *kṛtalakṣaṇa* and *ahatalakṣaṇa*.
(3.1.22) *Ibhya*, *āḍhya*, and *dhana* mean wealthy; *svāmin*, *īśvara*, *pati*, and *īśitṛ* mean master.
(3.1.23) *Adhibhū*, *nāyaka*, *netṛ*, *prabhu*, *parivṛḍha*, and *adhipa* mean leader or lord.

(3.1.24) One who is prosperous and wealthy, yet preoccupied with his family, is called an *abhyāgārika*. Furthermore, this term refers to a man who is endowed with excellent limbs and form, for he possesses the powerful build of a lion. (3.1.25–26) [Note: The numbering provided in the source text appears to be sequential across these verses.]
(3.1.27) One who is capable of performing his duty and endowed with excellence of character is called *nirvārya*.
(3.1.28) One who is silent and mute is called *avāci*, while one who is as swift as thought and resembles his father is called *pitṛsaṃnibha*.
(3.1.29) He who gives away a daughter adorned and honored is called a *kūkuda*.
(3.1.30) *Lakṣmīvān*, *lakṣmaṇaḥ*, *śrīlaḥ*, and *śrīmān* denote one who possesses fortune or beauty; *snigdhaḥ* and *vatsalaḥ* denote one who is affectionate.
(3.1.31) *Dayāluḥ*, *kāruṇikaḥ*, *kṛpāluḥ*, and *sūrataḥ* are synonymous terms for one who is compassionate.
(3.1.32) *Svatantro*, *apāvṛtaḥ*, *svairī*, *svacchandaḥ*, and *niravagrahaḥ* denote one who is independent or unrestrained.
(3.1.33) *Paratantra* means dependent on another, subject to another, or having a protector.
(3.1.34) *Adhīna*, *nighna*, *āyatta*, *asvacchanda*, and *gṛhyaka* also mean one who is under the control of another.
(3.1.35) A *khalapūḥ* is one who does much work; a *dīrghasūtraḥ* is one who is slow in action.
(3.1.36) *Jālma* refers to one who acts without reflection; *kuṇṭha* is one who is slow in actions.
(3.1.37) *Karmakṣama* is one capable of action; *alaṅkarmāṇa* is one intent on action; *kriyāvān* is one diligent in actions.
(3.1.38) *Kārma* is one whose habit is action; *karmaśūra* is a hero in action; *karmaṭha* is one devoted to work.
(3.1.39) A *bharaṇyabhuj* is a laborer; a *karmakāra*, however, is one who performs that specific work.
(3.1.40) An *apasnāta* is one who has bathed after a death; a *śauṣkala* is one who eats meat.
(3.1.41) One who is hungry is *bubhukṣita*; *kṣudhita* means the same; *jighatsu* and *aśanāyita* mean one who desires to eat.

(3.1.42) One who lives on the food of others, one who eats the morsels of others, a consumer, a glutton, or a voracious eater; (3.1.43) One who is devoid of the desire for conquest is called *ādyūna* or *audarika*; (3.1.44) Both *ātmambhari* and *kukṣimbhari* refer to one who fills his own belly.
(3.1.45) *Sarvānnīna* means one who eats all kinds of food; *gṛdhnu* means greedy (*gardhana*).
(3.1.46) *Lubdha* means covetous (*abhilāpuka*); *tṛṣṇak* is the same as *lolupa* and *lolubha*.
(3.1.47) *Sonmāda* means prone to madness (*unmadiṣṇu*); *avinīta* means arrogant (*samuddhata*).

(3.1.48) *śauṇḍa*, *utkaṭa*, and *kṣība* denote one who is intoxicated (*matte*); *kamitṛ*, *anuka*, (3.1.49) *kamra*, *kāmayitṛ*, *abhīka*, *kamana*, *kāmana*, and *abhika* denote a lover (*kāmuke*).
(3.1.50) *vidheya*, *vinayagrāhī*, *vacanastha*, and *āśrava* denote one who is obedient.
(3.1.51) *vaśya*, *praṇeya* mean "obedient"; *nibhṛta*, *vinīta*, and *praśrita* are synonyms meaning "modest.

(3.1.52) *dhṛṣṭa*, *dhṛṣṇu*, *viyāta*, and *pragalbha* denote one who is "bold" or "confident," while *pratibhānvita* means "possessed of presence of mind. (3.1.53) *adhṛṣṭa* refers to one who is "timid" or "bashful" (*śālīna*), whereas *vilakṣa* denotes one who is "filled with astonishment."
(3.1.54) *adhīra* means "faint-hearted"; *kātara*, *trasta*, *bhīru*, *bhīruka*, and *bhīluka* mean "timid.
(3.1.55) *āśaṃsuḥ* refers to one who desires; *āśaṃsitar* refers to one who hopes for something. *Gṛhayāluḥ* refers to one who seizes; *grahītṛ* refers to one who takes hold of.
(3.1.56) *Śraddhāluḥ* refers to one endowed with faith (*śraddhā*). *Patayāluḥ*, however, refers to one who falls (*pātuka*).

(3.1.57) *apatrapiṣṇu* means modest by nature; (3.1.58) *vandāru* means one who salutes or pays homage; *śarāru*, *ghātuka*, and *hiṃsra* mean murderous or injurious; *varddhiṣṇu* and *vardhana* mean increasing or growing;
(3.1.59) *utpatiṣṇu* means prone to leap up, while *alaṅkariṣṇu* means one who adorns or decorates.
(3.1.60) *bhūṣṇu* means one who desires to be; *śvaviṣṇu* means one who will be. *Vartiṣṇu* and *vartana* are synonyms for one who exists or persists.

(3.1.61) *Nirākariṣṇu* and *kṣipnu* mean one who rejects or casts aside. *Sāndrasnigdha* and *medura* mean thick and oily. (3.1.62) *Jñātṛ*, *vidura*, and *vindu* mean a knower. *Vikāsī* and *vikasvara* mean one who expands or blossoms.
(3.1.63) *visṛtvara*, *visṛmara*, and *prasārī* denote one who spreads or extends (*visārin*).
(3.1.64) *sahiṣṇu*, *sahana*, *kṣantṛ*, *titikṣu*, *kṣamitṛ*, and *kṣamī* denote one who endures or is patient.
(3.1.65) *krodhana*, *amarṣaṇa*, and *kopī* denote one who is prone to anger; *caṇḍa*, however, denotes one who is excessively irritable.

(3.1.66) *jāgarūka* means wakeful; *ghūrṇita* and *pracalāyita* mean drowsy. (3.1.67) *svapnak*, *śayālu*, and *nidrālu* mean sleepy; *nidrāṇa* and *śayita* are synonyms for one who is asleep. (3.1.68) *parāṅmukha* and *parācīna* mean turned away; *avāṅ* and *adhomukha* mean facing downwards.
(3.1.69) One who goes toward the gods is *devadryaṅ*; one who goes toward all directions is *viśvadryaṅ*.
(3.1.70) One who goes together is *sadhryaṅ*; one who goes crosswise is *tiryaṅ*.
(3.1.71) A speaker is *vadaḥ*, *vadāvadaḥ*, *vaktā*, *vāgīśaḥ*, and *vākpatiḥ*—these two are synonyms.
(3.1.72) One who is skillful in speech is called *vācoyukti-paṭu*, *vāgmī*, or *vāvadūka*; the last term refers to one who speaks excessively.

(3.1.73) A chatterer is *jalpāka*, while *vācāla* and *vācāṭa* refer to one whose speech is full of reproach. (3.1.74) *Durmukha*, *mukhara*, and *abaddhamukha* denote a foul-mouthed person; *śakta* refers to one who speaks kindly.
(3.1.75) One who speaks indistinctly is *lohalaḥ*; one who speaks reproachfully is *kadvadaḥ*. (3.1.76) *Kuvāda* and *kucara* are synonyms; one with an unpleasant voice is *asvaraḥ*.
(3.1.77) *Ravaṇaḥ* and *śabdanaḥ* mean the same; *nāndīvādī* and *nāndīkaraḥ* are synonyms for one who utters auspicious words.
(3.1.78) *Jaḍa* means ignorant; *eḍamūka*, however, refers to one untrained in speaking or hearing.
(3.1.79) One whose nature is silence is *tūṣṇīka*; *nagna* is one without clothes, i.e., naked (*digambara*).
(3.1.80) *Niṣkāsita* means expelled; *avakṛṣṭa* is the same; whereas *apadhvasta* means one who has been censured (*dhikkṛta*).
(3.1.81) *Āttagarva* means one who has been overcome; *dāpita* and *sādhita* are synonyms.
(3.1.82) *Pratyādiṣṭa* means rejected; *nirasta*, *pratyākhyāta*, and *nirākṛta* are synonyms.
(3.1.83) *Nikṛta* means treated with contempt; *viprakṛta* is the same; whereas *vipralabdha* means deceived.
(3.1.84) He who is struck down by the mind is *manohataḥ*, *pratihataḥ*, *pratibaddhaḥ*, and *hataḥ*.
(3.1.85) *Adhikṣiptaḥ* and *pratikṣiptaḥ* mean reviled; for one who is bound, the terms *kīlitaḥ* and *saṃyataḥ* are used.
(3.1.86) *Āpannaḥ* means one who has met with calamity (*āpatprāptaḥ*); *kāndiśīkaḥ* refers to one who has fled in fear.
(3.1.87) *Ākṣāritaḥ* and *kṣāritaḥ* mean one who is accused; *saṃkasukaḥ* means unstable.
(3.1.88) *Vyasanārtaḥ* and *uparaktaḥ* are two terms for one afflicted by calamity; *vihastaḥ* and *vyākulaḥ* are synonyms.
(3.1.89) *Viklavaḥ* and *vihvalaḥ* mean distressed; *vivaśaḥ* refers to one whose mind is corrupted by misfortune (*ariṣṭa*).
(3.1.90) *Kaśyaḥ* refers to one who deserves a whip; *tvātatāyī* refers to one who is armed and intent on killing.

(3.1.91) *Akṣigataḥ* means one who is detested; *vadhyah* and *śīrṣacchedyaḥ* are synonymous, meaning one deserving of death. (3.1.92) *Viṣyaḥ* is one who is to be killed by poison; *musalyaḥ* is one who is to be killed with a club.
(3.1.93) *Śiśvidāna* means one who has not performed black deeds; *capala* and *cikura* are synonyms.
(3.1.94) *Doṣaikadṛk* and *purobhāgī* mean one who sees only faults; *nikṛta*, *anṛju*, and *śaṭha* mean one who is crooked or deceitful.
(3.1.95) *Karṇejapa*, *sūcaka*, *piśuna*, *durjana*, and *khala* denote a malicious person or slanderer.
(3.1.96) *nṛśaṃsa* means cruel; *ghātuka* means murderous; *krūra* means fierce; *pāpa* means wicked; and *dhūrta* means a rogue or a deceiver.
(3.1.97) *ajña*, *mūḍha*, *yathājāta*, *mūrkha*, *vaidheya*, and *bāliśa* all mean ignorant or foolish.
(3.1.98) *kadarya*, *kṛpaṇa*, *kṣudra*, *kiṃpacāna*, and *amitampaca* all refer to a miser.
(3.1.99) But one who is without wealth is *niḥsva*; he is also called *durvidha*, *dīna*, *daridra*, and *durgata*.
(3.1.100) A beggar is a *vanīyaka*, a *yācanaka*, a *mārgaṇa*, a *yācaka*, or an *arthin*.
(3.1.101) One possessed of egoism is *ahaṅkāravat* or *ahaṃyuḥ*; one endowed with auspiciousness is *śubhaṃyuḥ*.
(3.1.102) The gods are born by divine apparition; humans, cattle, and so forth are born from the womb;
(3.1.103) worms, gadflies, and the like are born from sweat; birds, snakes, and so forth are born from eggs.
Thus ends the section on living beings; here there are fifty root verses.
(3.1.104) *Udbhidaḥ* refers to trees, shrubs, and the like; *udbhijjam* and *udbhidam* mean that which grows from the earth.
(3.1.105) *Sundaram*, *ruciram*, *cāru*, *suṣamam*, *sādhu*, and *śobhanam* mean beautiful.
(3.1.106) *Kāntam*, *manoramam*, *rucyam*, *manojñam*, *mañju*, and *mañjulam* mean lovely.
(3.1.107) *Ramya*, *manohara*, *saumya*, *bhadraka*, and *ramaṇīyaka* mean beautiful or charming.
(3.1.108) *Tadāsecanaka* refers to that which one never tires of beholding.
(3.1.109) *Abhīṣṭa*, *abhīpsita*, *hṛdya*, *dayita*, *vallabha*, and *priya* denote what is desired or beloved.
(3.1.110) *nikṛṣṭa*, *pratikṛṣṭa*, *arvā*, *repha*, *yāpya*, *avama*, and *adhama* [are synonyms for "low"].
(3.1.111) *kupūya*, *kutsita*, *avadya*, *kheṭa*, *garhya*, and *aṇaka* are synonymous.
(3.1.112) *malīmasa*, *malina*, *kaccara*, and *maladūṣita* [mean "soiled" or "dirty"].
(3.1.113) *pūta*, *pavitra*, and *medhya* mean pure; *vīdhra*, however, has the sense of being stainless.
(3.1.114) *nirṇikta*, *śodhita*, and *mṛṣṭa* mean cleansed; *niḥśodhya* and *anavaskara* mean free from impurity.
(3.1.115) *asāra*, *phalgu*, and *śūnya* mean worthless; *vaśika* and *tucchaka* mean empty.
(3.1.116) In the neuter gender, the words *pradhāna*, *pramukha*, *praveka*, *anuttama*, and *uttama* [denote the chief];
(3.1.117) as well as *mukhya*, *varya*, *vareṇya*, *pravara*, *anavara*, and *ardhya*;
(3.1.118) *parārdhya*, *agra*, *prāgrahara*, *prāgraya*, *agrya*, *agrīya*, and *agriya*.
(3.1.119) *Śreyas*, *śreṣṭha*, and *puṣkala* mean "excellent"; *sattama* is used for that which is most beautiful.

(3.1.120) In the position of a final member (*uttarapada*), the words *vyāghra*, *puṅgava*, *ṛṣabha*, and *kuñjara*—(3.1.121)—as well as *siṃha*, *śārdūla*, *nāga*, and others, when masculine, have the sense of "foremost" or "best."
(3.1.122) *aprāgryam* refers to two [words] that are devoid of excellence, namely those that are non-primary (*apradhāna*) and subordinate (*upasarjana*).
(3.1.123) *viśaṅkaṭa*, *pṛthu*, *bṛhat*, *viśāla*, *pṛthula*, and *mahat* mean wide, broad, or great.
(3.1.124) *vaḍra*, *uru*, and *vipula* mean vast; whereas *pīna* and *pīvra* mean thick or stout, while *sthūla* and *pīvara* mean fat or bulky.

(3.1.125) *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṣullaka*, *sūkṣma*, *ślakṣṇa*, *dabhra*, *kṛśa*, *tanu*; (3.1.126) *mātrā* and *truṭi* are feminine; *lava*, *leśa*, *kaṇa*, and *aṇu* are masculine; (3.1.127) for that which is extremely small, there are *alpiṣṭha*, *alpīyaḥ*, *kanīyaḥ*, and also *aṇīyaḥ*.
(3.1.128) *prabhūtam*, *pracuram*, *prājyam*, *adabhram*, *bahulam*, *bahu*; (3.1.129) *puruhūḥ*, *puru*, *bhūyiṣṭham*, *sphāram*, *bhūyaḥ*, and *bhūri*;
(3.1.130) those beginning with *paraḥ-śata* are [compounds] whose final member is a number such as "hundred" (*śata*) or the like.

(3.1.131) But *gaṇanīya* means "to be counted," while *gaṇeya* and *gaṇita* mean "counted. Furthermore, *sama*, *sarva*, (3.1.132) *viśva*, *aśeṣa*, *kṛtsna*, *samasta*, *nikhila*, *akhila*, *niḥśeṣa*,
(3.1.133) *samagra*, *sakala*, *pūrṇa*, and *akhaṇḍa* are used for that which is without deficiency.
(3.1.134) *Ghana* means continuous, dense, and thick; *pelava* means sparse, thin, and slight.
(3.1.135) *Samīpa*, *nikaṭa*, *āsanna*, *saṃnikṛṣṭa*, and *sanīḍavat* mean near.
(3.1.136) *Sadeśa*, *abhyāśa*, *savidha*, *samaryāda*, and *saveśavat* also mean near.

(3.1.137) *upakaṇṭha*, *antikā*, *abhyarṇa*, and *abhyagra* are synonyms for "near"; (3.1.138) *abhitaḥ* is also an indeclinable [used in this sense]. (3.1.139) Furthermore, *saṃsakta* means "contiguous," as do *avyavahita* and *apadāntara*.
*Nediṣṭha* and *antikama* mean "nearest," while *dūra* and *viprakṛṣṭaka* mean "far."
(3.1.140) *Davīyas* and *daviṣṭham* mean very far; *sudūra*, *dīrgha*, and *āyata* mean long.
(3.1.141) *Vartula*, *nistala*, and *vṛtta* mean round; *bandhura* means unevenly elevated and depressed.
(3.1.142) *Ucca*, *prāṃśu*, *unnata*, *udagra*, and *ucchrita* mean high; *tuṅga* likewise; whereas *vāmana* means short.
(3.1.143) *nyaṅ*, *nīca*, *kharva*, and *hrasva* denote what is low; *avāgra*, *avanata*, and *ānata* denote what is bent downward.
(3.1.144) *Arāla*, *vṛjina*, *jihma*, *ūrmita*, *kuñcita*, and *nata* denote what is curved.
(3.1.145) *Āviddha*, *kuṭila*, *bhugna*, *vellita*, and *vakra* also denote what is crooked.

(3.1.146) *Ṛju* means straight or honest; *ajihma* and *praguṇa* have the same meaning. Conversely, *apraguṇa* and *ākula* mean crooked or confused. (3.1.147) *Śāśvata*, *dhruva*, *nitya*, *sadātana*, and *sanātana* all mean eternal or perpetual.
(3.1.148) *Sthāsnu* means very firm or stable; however, that which remains in one and the same form is called *stheyas*.
(3.1.149) That which pervades time is immovable, stable, and other than mobile;
(3.1.150) moving, mobile, wandering, trembling, and that which moves and does not move;
(3.1.151) shifting, shaking, tremulous, moving, wavering, and unstable.
(3.1.152) *cañcala* and *tarala* mean flickering; *pāriplava* and *pariplava* mean wavering.
(3.1.153) *atirikta* and *samadhika* mean excessive; *dhṛḍhasandhi* and *saṃhata* mean firm-jointed or compact.
(3.1.154) *khakkhaṭa*, *kaṭhina*, *krūra*, *kaṭhora*, *niṣṭhura*, and *dhṛḍha* mean hard or rigid.
(3.1.155) *jaraṭham*, *mūrtimat*, *mūrtam*, *pravṛddham*, *prauḍham*, *edhitam* [mean "grown old" or "firm"];
(3.1.156) *purāṇa*, *pratana*, *pratna*, *purātana*, *cirantana* [mean "ancient"]; (3.1.157) *pratyagra*, *abhinava*, *navya*, *navīna*, *nūtana*, *nava* [mean "new"].

(3.1.158) *nūtna* means new; *sukumāra*, *komala*, *mṛdula*, and *mṛdu* mean soft. (3.1.159) *anvaga*, *anvakṣam*, *anuga*, and *anupadam* are indeclinables used as neuters meaning "following after. (3.1.160) *pratyakṣa* refers to that which is perceptible by the senses (*aindriyaka*), while *apratyakṣa* refers to that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
(3.1.161) *Ekatāna* means having no other activity; it also refers to *aikāgra* and *ekāyana*. (3.1.162) He is also called *ekasarga*, *ekāgrya*, and *ekāyanagata*.
(3.1.163) *Ādi*, *pūrva*, *paurastya*, *prathama*, and *ādya* are masculine; furthermore, they are neuter when not feminine.
(3.1.164) *anta*, *jaghanya*, *carama*, *antya*, *pāścātya*, and *paścima* mean "last" or "final.

(3.1.165) *Mogha*, *nirarthaka*, *spaṣṭa*, *sphuṭa*, *pravyakta*, and *ulbaṇa* mean "clear," "evident," or "manifest. (3.1.166) *Sādhāraṇa* and *sāmānya* mean "common" or "shared," while *ekākī*, *eka*, and *ekaka* mean "solitary" or "alone."
(3.1.167) *anyatara* and *ekataḥ* [are used] when there is a distinction of meaning; *anyetara* is also [used in this sense].
(3.1.168) *Uccāvaca* means having many varieties; *uccaṇḍa* means not slow.
(3.1.169) *Aruntuda* means piercing the vital spots (*marmaspṛś*); *abādha* means unrestrained (*nirargala*).
(3.1.170) *Prasavya* means contrary or unfavorable; it also means *apasavya* and *apaṣṭhu*.
(3.1.171) On the body, *savya* refers to the left side, while *apasavya* refers to the right.
(3.1.172) *Saṅkaṭa* and *saṃbādha* mean narrow or crowded; *kalila* and *gahana* are synonyms for dense or impenetrable.
(3.1.173) *saṃkīrṇa* means crowded or filled; *muṇḍita* means shorn or shaved.
(3.1.174) *granthita*, *sandita*, *dṛbdha*, *visṛta*, *vistṛta*, and *tata* mean knotted or woven.
(3.1.175) *antargata* means forgotten; *prāpta* and *praṇihita* are synonyms meaning obtained or placed.

(3.1.176) *vellita*, *preṅkhita*, *ādhūta*, *calita*, and *ākampita* are synonyms for *dhuta* (shaken). (3.1.177) *nutta*, *nūna*, *asta*, *niṣṭhyūta*, *āviddha*, *kṣipta*, and *īrita* are synonyms. (3.1.178) *parikṣipta* is synonymous with *nivṛtta*; *mūṣita* has the same meaning as *muṣita* (stolen).

(3.1.179) *pravṛddha* and *prasṛta* [are used] for *nyasta* and *nisṛṣṭa*; (3.1.180) *guṇita* and *āhata* [are used] for *nidigdha* and *upacita*; *gūḍha* and *gupta* [are used] for *guṇṭhita* and *rūṣita*;
(3.1.181) *druta* and *avadīrṇa* [are used] for *udgūrṇa* and *udyata*; *kācita* and *śikyita* [are used] for these same pairs.
(3.1.182) *ghrāta* means smelled; *digdha* and *lipta* mean smeared; *samudakta* and *uddhṛta* mean drawn up or lifted out; *sama* means level or equal.
(3.1.183) *veṣṭita*, *valayita*, *saṃvīta*, *ruddha*, and *āvṛta* mean encircled, wound, enveloped, obstructed, or covered.
(3.1.184) *rugṇa* and *bhugna* mean bent; furthermore, *niśita*, *kṣṇuta*, *śāta*, and *atejita* mean sharpened.

(3.1.185) *pakva* means ready for destruction; *hrīṇa* and *hrīta* mean ashamed. (3.1.186) *vṛtta* and *vṛtavyāvṛtta* mean one who has performed his duty; *saṃyojita* and *upāhita* mean joined together.
(3.1.187) *prāpya*, *gamya*, and *samāsādya* mean reachable; *syanna*, *rīṇa*, *snuta*, and *sruta* mean flowed.

(3.1.188) *saṃgūḍhaḥ* means "calculated" (*saṃkalitaḥ*); *avagītaḥ* means "one whose reproach is well-known" (*khyātagarhaṇaḥ*). (3.1.189) *vividhaḥ*, *bahuvidhaḥ*, *nānārūpaḥ*, and *pṛthagvidhaḥ* all mean "of various kinds.
(3.1.190) *avarīṇaḥ* means "reviled" (*dhikkṛtaḥ*); it also means "crushed" (*avadhvastaḥ*) or "pulverized" (*avacūrṇitaḥ*).

(3.1.191) *Phāṇṭa* refers to that which is prepared without effort; *svanita* and *dhvanita* are synonyms. (3.1.192) When bound, it is called *sandānitam*, *mūtam*, *udditam*, *sanditam*, and *sitam*. (3.1.193) That which is thoroughly cooked is *kvathitam*; in the sense of cooking, the words *śṛtam* are used for milk, clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
(3.1.194) *Nirvāṇa* is used for a sage, fire, and so forth; *nirvāta*, however, means when the wind has ceased.
(3.1.195) *Pakva* means matured or ripened; *gūna* means killed; *mīḍha* means urinated. (3.1.196) *Puṣita* means nourished; *kṣānta* means endured; *udvānta* means vomited.

(3.1.197) *dānta* is used for one who has been tamed (*damita*); *śānta* for one who has been calmed (*śamita*); *ardita* for one who has been afflicted (*prārthita*). (3.1.198) *jñapta* is used for one who has been made known (*jñāpita*); *channa* for one who has been covered (*chādita*); *añcita* for one who has been honored (*pūjita*). (3.1.199) *pūrṇa* is used for one who has been filled (*pūrita*); *kliṣṭa* for one who has been afflicted (*kliśita*); *sita* for one who has ceased (*avasita*).
(3.1.200) *Pruṣṭa*, *pluṣṭa*, and *uṣita* denote that which is burnt; *taṣṭa* and *tvaṣṭa* denote that which has been made thin.
(3.1.201) *Vedhita* and *cchidrita* denote that which is pierced; *vinna* and *vitta* denote that which is investigated.
(3.1.202) *Niṣprabha* and *vigatāroka* denote that which is lusterless; *vilīna*, *vidruta*, and *druta* denote that which is melted.
(3.1.203) *Siddha*, *nirvṛtta*, and *niṣpanna* denote that which is accomplished; *dārita*, *bhinna*, and *bhedita* denote that which is split.
(3.1.204) The triad *ūta*, *syūta*, and *uta* refers to what is woven with threads.
(3.1.205) *Namasyita*, *namasita*, *apacāyita*, *arcita*, and *apacita* are used for one who is worthy of honor.
(3.1.206) *varivasita*, *varivasyita*, *upāsita*, and *upacarita* [are synonyms for "served"];
(3.1.207) *saṃtāpita*, *saṃtapta*, *dhūpita*, *dhūpāyita*, and *dūna* [are synonyms for "tormented"];
(3.1.208) *hṛṣṭa*, *matta*, *tṛpta*, *prahlanna*, *pramudita*, and *prīta* [are synonyms for "delighted"].
(3.1.209) *chinnaṃ*, *chātaṃ*, *lūnaṃ*, *kṛttaṃ*, *dātaṃ*, *ditaṃ*, *chitaṃ*, *vṛkṇam* (cut);
(3.1.210) *srastaṃ*, *dhvastaṃ*, *bhraṣṭaṃ*, *skannaṃ*, *pannaṃ*, *cyutaṃ*, *galitam* (fallen, dropped, fallen away, flowed out, perished, slipped, melted away);
(3.1.211) *labdhaṃ*, *prāptaṃ*, *vinnaṃ*, *bhāvitaṃ*, *āsāditaṃ*, and *bhūtam* (obtained, attained, found, brought about, reached, and come into being).

(3.1.212) *anveṣitam*, *gaveṣitam*, *anviṣṭam*, *mārgitam*, *mṛgitam*; (3.1.213) *ārdram*, *sārdram*, *klinnam*, *timitam*, *smititam*, *samunnatam*, *uttam* ca; (3.1.214) *trātam*, *trāṇam*, *rakṣitam*, *avitam*, *gopāyitam*, and *guptam*.
(3.1.215) *Avagaṇita*, *avamata*, *avajñāta*, and *avamānita* mean despised or insulted;
(3.1.216) *tyakta*, *hīna*, *vidhuta*, *samujjhita*, *dhūta*, and *utsṛṣṭa* mean abandoned;
(3.1.217) *ukta*, *bhāṣita*, *udita*, *jalpita*, *ākhyāta*, *abhihita*, and *lapita* mean spoken.
(3.1.218) *buddham*, *budhitam*, *manitam*, *viditam*, *pratipannam*, *avasitam*, *avagatam*;
(3.1.219) *urīkṛtam*, *urarīkṛtam*, *aṅgīkṛtam*, *āśrutam*, *pratijñātam*;
(3.1.220) *saṃgīrṇam*, *viditam*, *saṃśrutam*, *samāhitam*, *upaśrutam*, *upagatam*.
(3.1.221) *īlita*, *śasta*, *paṇāyita*, *panāyita*, *praṇuta*, *paṇita*, and *panita*;
(3.1.222) furthermore, *gīrṇa*, *varṇita*, *abhiṣṭuta*, and *iḍita* have the meaning of "praised";
(3.1.223) *bhakṣita*, *carvita*, *lipta*, *pratyavasita*, *gilita*, *khādita*, and *psāta*.
(3.1.224) *abhyavahṛta*, *annajagdha*, *grasta*, *glasta*, and *aśita* are used in the sense of "eaten" (*bhukta*).
(3.1.225) *kṣepiṣṭha*, *kṣodiṣṭha*, *preṣṭha*, *variṣṭha*, *sthaviṣṭha*, and *baṃhiṣṭha* [are superlative forms].

(3.1.226) These [superlatives] have as their meanings the excellence (*prakarṣa*) of speed (*kṣipra*), smallness (*kṣudra*), that which is desired (*abhīpsita*), largeness (*pṛthu*), stoutness (*pīvara*), and abundance (*bahula*).

(3.1.227) *sādhiṣṭha-drāghiṣṭha-spheṣṭha-gariṣṭha-hrasiṣṭha-vṛndiṣṭhāḥ* (3.1.228) [are used] in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*) regarding the firm (*bāḍha*), the long (*vyāyata*), the much (*bahu*), the heavy (*guru*), the short (*vāmana*), and the excellent (*vṛndāraka*).
This concludes the section on words denoting the qualities of the objects qualified (*viśeṣyanighnavarga*). Here, verse 112 [of the root text].
The Section on Miscellaneous Terms (Saṃkīrṇavarga).
(3.2.229) One should infer the gender in the case of miscellaneous [terms] by means of the meaning of the root, the suffix, and so forth.
Now begins the Section on Miscellaneous Terms.
(3.2.230) When the continuity of an action (*kriyā*) is to be understood, the term *aparaspara* may be used. (3.2.231) *Pārāyaṇa* and *parāyaṇa* denote completeness and non-attachment, respectively.
(3.2.232) *Yadṛcchā* means acting according to one's own will; it is a state devoid of a specific cause, whereas *āsthā* is its opposite.

(3.2.233) *Śama* is tranquility (*śama*), peace (*śānti*); *dānti* is self-restraint (*damatha*), subduing (*dama*). (3.2.234) *Avadāna* is a deed or conduct; *pravāraṇa* is a desired gift. (3.2.235) *Saṃvanana* is the act of bringing under control; *mūlakarma*, however, is *kārmaṇa*.
(3.2.236) *vidhūnanam* and *vidhuvanam* mean shaking; *tarpaṇam*, *prīṇanam*, and *āvanam* mean satisfying.
(3.2.237) *paryāptiḥ*, *paritrāṇam*, and *hastadhāraṇam* also denote protection or support.
(3.2.238) *sevanam*, *sīvanam*, and *syūtiḥ* mean sewing; *vidaraḥ*, *sphuṭanam*, and *bhidā* mean bursting or cleaving.
(3.2.239) *Ākrośanam* is reviling; *abhīṣaṅgaḥ* is attachment. *Saṃvedaḥ* and *vedanā* are synonyms for feeling (*na nā*).

(3.2.240) *Saṃmūrcchanam* is pervasion; *yāñcā*, *bhikṣā*, *arthanā*, and *ardanā* are synonyms for begging. (3.2.241) *Vardhanam* means cutting; furthermore, there are two terms for gladdening and honoring.
(3.2.242) *Āpracchanna* means tradition (*āmnāya*) or lineage (*saṃpradāya*); *kṣiyā* occurs in the sense of decay (*kṣaya*).
(3.2.243) *Grāha* occurs in the sense of seizing (*graha*); *vaśaḥ* in the sense of desire (*kānti*); *rakṣṇas* in the sense of protection (*trāṇa*); *raṇaḥ* in the sense of sound (*kaṇa*).
(3.2.244) *Vyadhaḥ* in the sense of piercing (*vedha*); *pacaḥ* in the sense of cooking (*pāka*); *havaḥ* in the sense of invocation (*hūti*); *varaḥ* in the sense of choosing (*vṛtti*).

(3.2.245) *Oṣaḥ* means burning; *nayaḥ* means leading; *jyāniḥ* means decay; *bhramaḥ* and *bhramau* mean wandering. (3.2.246) *Sphātiḥ* means growth; *prathā* means fame; *spṛṣṭiḥ* means contact; *snavaḥ* means flowing. (3.2.247) *Edhāḥ* means prosperity; *sphuraṇā* means throbbing; *pramā* means valid cognition.
(3.2.248) *prasūtiḥ* [is used] in the sense of procreation; *prādhāraḥ* in the sense of dripping; *klamathaḥ* in the sense of exhaustion.

(3.2.249) *utkarṣaḥ* in the sense of excellence; *saṃdhiḥ* in the sense of joining; *viṣayaḥ* in the sense of a locus or support. (3.2.250) *kṣepaṇam* in the sense of casting away; *gīrṇiḥ* in the sense of swallowing; *guraṇam* in the sense of exertion.
(3.2.251) *unnāya* means "raising up" (*unnaye*); *śrāya* means "relying upon" (*śrayaṇe*); and *jaya* means "victory" (*jayane*).
(3.2.252) *nigāda* means "recitation" (*nigade*); *māda* means "intoxication" (*mada*); and *udvega* means "agitation" (*udbhrame*).
(3.2.253) *vimardana* means "rubbing" (*parimala*); and *anugraha* means "favor" (*abhyupapatti*).
(3.2.254) *Nigraha* is its opposite; *abhiyoga*, however, is *abhigraha*.
(3.2.255) *Muṣṭibandha* is *saṃgrāha*; *ḍimba* refers to a riot, while *ḍamara* and *viplava* denote a tumultuous disturbance.
(3.2.256) *Bandhana*, *prasiti*, and *cāra* mean binding; *sparśa* refers to one who touches, while *upataptṛ* refers to one who causes affliction.
(3.2.257) *Nikāra* and *viprakāra* mean insult; *ākāra*, however, means a sign or gesture (*iṅga*, *iṅgita*).
(3.2.258) *Pariṇāma* and *vikāra* are two terms for transformation; *vikṛti* and *vikriyā* are likewise synonymous.
(3.2.259) *Apahāra* and *apacaya* mean loss or decrease; *samāhāra* and *samuccaya* mean collection or accumulation.

(3.2.260) *Pratyāhāra* means taking up; *vihāra*, however, means wandering. (3.2.261) *Abhihāra* is seizing; *nihāra* is drawing away or removal. (3.2.262) *Anuhāra* is imitation; *vyaya* is the depletion of wealth.
(3.2.263) *Pravāha* is *pravṛtti*; *pravaha* is going outside.
(3.2.264) *Vi-yāma*, *vi-yama*, *yāma*, *yama*, *saṃ-yāma*, and *saṃ-yama*.
(3.2.265) *Abhicāra* is a rite of injury; *jāgaryā* and *jāgara* are both [terms for] wakefulness.
(3.2.266) *Vighna*, *antarāya*, and *pratyūha* mean an obstacle; *upaghna* means that which is near or a shelter.
(3.2.267) *Nirveśa* means enjoyment; *parisarpa* means service or attendance. (3.2.268) *Vidhura* refers to separation; *abhiprāya*, *chanda*, and *āśaya* mean intention or purpose.
(3.2.269) *Saṃkṣepaṇa*, *samasana*, *paryavasthā*, and *virodhana* mean contraction. (3.2.270) *Parisaryā* and *parīsāra* mean wandering about; whereas *āsya*, *āsanā*, and *sthiti* mean sitting.
(3.2.271) *Vistāra*, *vigraha*, and *vyāsa* mean expansion, and that [term] also refers to the elaboration of a word.

(3.2.272) *Saṃvāhana* means massaging; *vināśa* means disappearance. (3.2.273) *Saṃstava* means acquaintance; *prasara*, however, means spreading. (3.2.274) *Nīvāka* means expenditure; *saṃnidhi* means proximity.
(3.2.275) *lava* means desire; *lavana* is threshing, and *pavana* is winnowing;
*pava*. (3.2.276) *prastāva* refers to a prelude; *trasara* is the winding of thread.
(3.2.277) *prajana* is mating; *upasara*; *praśraya* and *praṇaya* are synonyms for courtesy or affection.
(3.2.278) *Dhīśakti* is intellect; *niṣkrama* is departure; *saṃkrama*, however, is not feminine and means a difficult passage.
(3.2.279) *Pratyutkrama* is for the purpose of application; *prakrama* and *upakrama* are synonyms.
(3.2.280) *Abhyādāna*, *uddhāta*, and *ārambha* are synonyms; *saṃbhrama* and *tvarā* mean haste.
(3.2.281) *Pratibandhaḥ* means obstruction; *pratiṣṭambhaḥ* means resistance; *avanāyaḥ*, however, means causing to fall down.
(3.2.282) *Upalambhaḥ* means experience; *samālambhaḥ* means anointing.
(3.2.283) *Vipralambhaḥ* means separation; *vilambhaḥ*, however, means giving away.
(3.2.284) *viśrāva* and *pratikhyāti* mean fame; *avekṣā* and *pratijāgara* mean watchfulness.
(3.2.285) *nipāṭha* and *nipaṭha* refer to recitation; *tema* and *stema* refer to moistening.
(3.2.286) *ādīnava* and *āsrava* refer to affliction; *mela* and *saṅga-saṅgama* refer to meeting or union.
(3.2.287) *saṃvīkṣaṇaṃ*, *vicayanaṃ*, *mārgaṇaṃ*, *mṛgaṇā*, and *mṛgaḥ* [mean searching].
(3.2.288) *parirambhaḥ*, *pariṣvaṅgaḥ*, *saṃśleṣaḥ*, and *upagūhanam* [mean embracing].
(3.2.289) *nirvarṇanam*, *nidhyānam*, *darśanam*, *ālokanaṃ*, and *īkṣaṇam* [mean gazing or beholding].
(3.2.290) *Pratyākhyānam*, *nirasanam*, *pratyādeśaḥ*, and *nirākṛtiḥ* [are synonyms for rejection].
(3.2.291) *Upaśāyaḥ* and *viśāyaḥ* have the meaning of lying down in turn (*paryāyaśayana*).
(3.2.292) *Artanam*, *ṛtīyā*, and *hṛṇīyā* have the meaning of disgust (*ghṛṇā*).

(3.2.293) *Vyatyāsa*, *viparyāsa*, and *vyatyaya* occur in the sense of reversal (*viparyaya*). (3.2.294) *Paryaya*, *atikrama*, *atipāta*, and *upātyaya* occur in that same sense. (3.2.295) That which is an ordering by summoning is *pratiśāsana*.
(3.2.296) That place where the twice-born offer praise during sacrifices is called *saṃstāva*.
(3.2.297) Where one piece of wood is placed against another and shaped, that is called *uddhana*.
(3.2.298) A *stambaghna* or *stambaghana* is that by which a thicket (*stamba*) is struck down.
(3.2.299) *Āvidha* is that by which one is pierced; in this regard, when [the action] is performed all around (*viṣvaksama*), it is *nigha*.
(3.2.300) Both *utkāra* and *nikāra* have the sense of tossing up grain. (3.2.301) *Nigāra*, *udgāra*, *vikṣāva*, and *udgrāha*, however, refer to swallowing and so forth.

(3.2.302) *Ārati*, *avarati*, and *virati* denote cessation; furthermore, *niṣṭhyūtiḥ* is used in the non-feminine gender. (3.2.303) *Niṣṭhyūtiḥ*, *niṣṭhevana*, and *niṣṭhīvana* are synonymous. (3.2.304) *Jūtiḥ* denotes speed, while *sātiḥ* occurs at the end [of a sacrifice]; furthermore, *jūrtiḥ* denotes fever.
(3.2.305) *udāja* and *paśupreraṇa*, as well as *makarandī* and so forth, [are used] in the sense of a curse;
(3.2.306) from those ending in *gotra*, in the sense of "a collection thereof," there are forms such as *aupagavaka*;
(3.2.307) likewise, *āpūpikaṃ* and *śāṣkulikam* and so forth [denote collections] of insentient things.
(3.2.308) *māṇavyam* is [the collective] of *māṇavas*, and *sahāyatā* is [the collective] of *sahāyas*;

(3.2.309) *halyā* is [the collective] of *halas*, while *brāhmaṇyam* and *vāḍavyam* are [the collectives] of the twice-born; (3.2.310) *parśu* and *pārśvam* are [the collectives] of the ribs (*parśukās*), and *pṛṣṭhya* is [the collective] of the backs (*pṛṣṭhas*) in due order.
(3.2.311) From *khala* comes *khalinī* and also *khalyā*; likewise, *mānuṣyaka* [denotes] a collection of men (*nṛṇām*).
(3.2.312) Similarly, *grāmatā*, *janatā*, *dhūmyā*, *pāśyā*, and *galyā* each denote a collection of villages, people, smoke, snares, and throats respectively.
(3.2.313) Furthermore, there are forms such as *sāhasra*, *kārīṣa*, *vārmaṇa*, and *ātharvaṇa*.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous terms (saṃkīrṇavarga), the second; here there are 42 root verses.
Now begins the section on words of multiple meanings (nānārthavarga):
some words of multiple meanings have already been mentioned here within the sections on *kānta* and so forth.

Now, the section on words with multiple meanings (3.3.315): Those words which have extensive usage in certain [meanings] may also be used for their synonyms (3.3.316). *Nāka* refers to the sky or heaven (*tridiva*); *loka*, however, refers to the world (*bhuvana*) or people (*jana*).
(3.3.317) *Śloka* refers to a verse and fame; *sāyaka* refers to an arrow and a sword.
(3.3.318) *Jambuka* refers to a jackal and Varuṇa; *pṛthuka* refers to flattened rice and an infant.
(3.3.319) *Āloka* refers to sight and light; *bherī*, *paṭaha*, and *mānaka* refer to types of drums.
(3.3.320) *Aṅka* refers to the lap and a mark; *kalaṅka* refers to a spot and a reproach.
(3.3.321) *Takṣaka* refers to a serpent and a carpenter; *arka* refers to crystal and the sun.
(3.3.322) *Kaḥ* in the masculine denotes wind, Brahmā, and the sun; *kam* denotes the head and water.

(3.3.323) *Pulāka* may refer to empty grain, a concise summary, or a grain of boiled rice; (3.3.324) *Pecaka* refers to an owl or the tuft at the base of an elephant's tail; (3.3.325) *Karaka* refers to a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) or the Buddha (*sugata*); and *vināyaka* refers to the Buddha.
(3.3.326) *Kiṣku* refers to a cubit or a span; *vṛścika* refers to a scorpion or a silk-worm.
(3.3.327) *Pratīka* means adverse or hostile (used in three genders); it also denotes a single part (used in the masculine).
(3.3.328) *Bhūtika* refers to the *bhūnimba* plant, as well as *kattṛṇa* and *bhūstṛṇa*.
The word *jyotsnikā* refers to both a cowherd settlement (*ghoṣa*) and the plant *kośātakī*; furthermore, *kaṭphala* refers to the fruit of the *kaṭphala* tree.
(3.3.330) The term *somavalka* denotes both the white variety of the *khadira* tree and the plant *sihvaka*.
(3.3.331) The word *piṇyāka* refers to both sesame paste and oil-cake; furthermore, *bāhlīka* refers to asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*). (3.3.331)

(3.3.332) *Kauśika* refers to Mahendra, guggulu, an owl, and a snake-catcher; (3.3.333) *ātaṅka* means pain, affliction, or apprehension; *kṣullaka* is used in three genders to mean even a very small thing; (3.3.334) *jaivātṛka* refers to the moon as well; *vartaka* refers to the hoof of a horse as well.
(3.3.335) *Puṇḍarīka* is used for a tiger as well; (3.3.336) *dīpaka* is used for *yavānī* as well; (3.3.337) *śālāvṛka* refers to a monkey, a jackal, and a dog; *gairika* is used for gold as well;
*vyalīka* may mean harm, while *alīka* means unpleasant or untrue.
(3.3.338) *śīla* and *anvaya* are two [synonyms] for *anūka*; *śalka* refers to a splinter, a bark, or a scale.
(3.3.339) *Niṣka* is used for one hundred and eight *suvarṇas*, for gold, for a breast ornament, and for a *pala*.
It is also used for a *dīnāra*. *Kalka* is not feminine; it denotes impurity or sin.
(3.3.341) Also, *pināka* denotes hypocrisy; furthermore, it is not feminine when referring to a trident or the bow of Śaṅkara.
(3.3.342) *Dhenukā*, however, refers to a female elephant; and *kālikā* refers to a mass of clouds.
(3.3.343) *Kārikā* refers to torture or a means of livelihood; *karṇikā* refers to an ornament for the ear.

(3.3.344) *karahasta* refers to a finger or the seed-vessel of a lotus; these three [meanings] follow. (3.3.345) *vṛndāraka* means beautiful or chief; *eka* means chief, other, or exclusive. (3.3.346) A hypocrite who keeps his eyes cast down is called a *kaukkuṭika*.

(3.3.347) *Lalāṭika* refers to one who watches the forehead of his master, i.e., one who is incapable of performing action; (3.3.348) and [the term *kaṭaka*] refers to the circles of the mountain ridges, being masculine and neuter; (3.3.349) [and it is] not feminine.
(3.3.350) *Kaṇṭaka* refers to the point of a needle, a petty enemy, and horripilation;
(3.3.351) *pāka* refers to cooking and a child; *nāyaka* refers to a central gem and a leader; (3.3.352) *paryaṅka* refers to a retinue and a couch; and *lubdhaka* refers to a hunter.
(3.3.353) *Peṭaka* is used in three senses: a multitude, a teacher, and a place to be shown.
(3.3.354) *Kheṭaka* refers to a village and a shield; *jālika* also refers to a fisherman.
(3.3.355) *Kiñjalka* refers to the filament of a flower and pollen; *śulka* is not feminine and also refers to a woman’s property.
(3.3.356) *Utkalikā* may mean a wave or longing; *vārdhakya* refers to old age or a multitude of states.
(3.3.357) *Gaṇikā* denotes a female elephant or a courtesan; *dāraka* means a child or a kind of tree.
(3.3.358) *Aneḍamūka* refers to one who is both deaf and mute; *ṭaṅka* denotes a chisel or a stone-splitting tool used for pride.
(3.3.359) *uṣṭrikā* refers to an earthen vessel; *mantha* is a churning stick; *khajaka* is a ladle for liquids.
(3.3.360) These end in the suffix *ka*.
(3.3.361) *Mayūkha*, *tviṭ*, *kiraṇa*, and *jvālā* mean a ray of light; *alī* and *bāṇa* are synonyms for *śilīmukha* (an arrow).

(3.3.362) *Śaṅkha* refers to a treasure, the frontal bone, and a conch-shell; it is not feminine. *Khā* also refers to an organ of sense. (3.3.363) *Śikhā* refers to a flame and a crest. *Naga* and *aga* refer to mountains and trees.
(3.3.364) Thus end the words ending in *kh*.
(3.3.365) *Āśuga* refers to both wind and an arrow; *khaga* denotes an arrow, the sun, and a bird.
(3.3.366) *Pataṅga* signifies both a bird and the sun; *pūga* refers to both the betel nut tree and a multitude.
(3.3.367) *Mṛga* also refers to domestic animals; *vega* denotes both a current and speed.
(3.3.368) *Parāga* refers to the pollen of flowers, as well as to dust such as that used for bathing;
(3.3.369) *nāga* and *mātaṅga* both refer to an elephant, while *apāṅga* refers to the outer corner of the eye and also to a sectarian mark (*tilaka*);
(3.3.370) *sarga* refers to innate nature, liberation, resolution, a chapter, and creation.
(3.3.371) *Yoga* [is used] in the senses of equipment, means, meditation, conjunction, and reasoning;
(3.3.372) *Bhoga* [is used] in the sense of pleasure, the maintenance of women and so forth, and the hood or body of a serpent;
(3.3.373) *Sāraṅga* [denotes] the *cātaka* bird and the deer in the masculine, and is used in the three genders for "variegated."
(3.3.374) *Plavaga* means a monkey; *abhiṣaṅga* means a curse or defeat.
(3.3.375) *Yuga* as a masculine noun refers to the pole of a vehicle and so forth; *yugam* (neuter) means a pair or the *Kṛta*-age and others.
(3.3.376) [The word *go*] signifies heaven, an arrow, cattle, speech, a thunderbolt, a direction, an eye, a ray, the earth, and water.
(3.3.377) From the perspective of its referent, *liṅga* denotes "female," "male," "cow," "mark," or "penis.
(3.3.378) *Śṛṅga* denotes "preeminence" and "summit"; *varāṅga* denotes "head" and "private parts.
(3.3.379) *Bhaga* denotes "fortune," "desire," "magnanimity," "heroism," "effort," "the sun," and "fame."
Thus end the words ending in *g*.

(3.3.381) *Parigha* refers to an obstruction and also to a type of weapon. *Ogha* refers to a multitude and the current of water. (3.3.382) *Argha* refers to price and the ritual of worship; *agha* refers to distress, suffering, and calamity.

(3.3.383) *laghu* means "light" in three senses: desired, small, and light [in weight]. (3.3.384) Words ending in *gha*: *kāca* means "glass" or "eye-disease"; *śikya* means "a sling" or "a net"; *mṛd-bheda* means "clay-division" or "earthenware"; *dṛg-ruj* means "eye-pain.
(3.3.385) *prapañca* means "reversal" or "elaboration"; *śuci* means "fire" or "pure."
(3.3.386) *māsya* means "minister" (*amātya*) and also "deceit" (*upadhā*); it is masculine. In the sense of "pure" (*medhya*) and "white" (*sita*), it is used in three genders.
(3.3.387) *Ruci* is feminine; it denotes "attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*), "desire" (*spṛhā*), and "ray" (*gabhasti*).
Thus end [the words] ending in *c*.
(3.3.389) *Accha* also means a clear or bright *bhallūka* (bear); *guccha* refers to a cluster (*stabaka*) or a pearl necklace (*hāra*).

(3.3.390) *Kaccha* refers to the hem of a lower garment; it is triliṅga (masculine, feminine, and neuter) when referring to the edge of water. (3.3.391) Thus end the inserted [terms] ending in *kaccha*.
(3.3.392) *Kekī* refers to a peacock; *tārkṣya*, a snake-eater; *dvija* refers to a tooth, a Brahmin, or a bird.
(3.3.393) *Aja* refers to Viṣṇu, Śiva, or a goat; *vraja* refers to a cow-pen, a path, or a multitude.
(3.3.394) *Dharmarāja* refers to the Jina or Yama; *kuñja* refers to a tusk, and is not feminine.

(3.3.395) *Valaja* refers to the gate of a field-fortress; *valajā* means having beautiful appearance. (3.3.396) *Āji* occurs in the sense of a level plot of land and also in the sense of battle; *prajā* occurs in the sense of progeny and people.
(3.3.397) *Abja* refers to the conch and the moon; *nija* means one's own and constant, and is used in three genders.
(3.3.398) Thus end the words ending in *j*.
(3.3.399) *Kṣetrajña* is used in the masculine sense for the self (*ātman*) and for one who is proficient; it is a term whose gender varies according to its referent.
(3.3.400) *Saṃjñā* is consciousness (*cetanā*), as well as the indication of meaning by means of the hands and other such gestures.

(3.3.401) *doṣajñau* refers to a physician and a scholar; (3.3.402) *jñaḥ* means a scholar and also the son of Soma (Budha); these end in the suffix *ñ*. (3.3.403) *karaṭau* refers to a crow and a temple of Gaṇeśa; *kaṭau* refers to the temples of an elephant and the hips.
(3.3.404) *Śipiviṣṭa* refers to one with a bald head, one with bad skin, or Maheśvara;
(3.3.405) *Tvaṣṭṛ* also refers to the divine artisan; *diṣṭa* refers to fate, but not in the sense of "two";
(3.3.406) *kaṭu* refers to a pungent taste; it is used in three genders for that which is harsh, envious, or sharp.
(3.3.407) *Ṛṣṭa* refers to security, the absence of good or evil; however, *ariṣṭa* refers to both good and evil omens.
(3.3.408) *Kūṭa* is used for illusions, stationary machines, deceit, falsehoods, and heaps; it is neuter.
(3.3.409) *Kūṭa* is also used for an iron mace, a mountain peak, and a part of a plough; it is not feminine.
(3.3.410) *truṭi* is feminine in the sense of small cardamom; it also denotes a short time or doubt.
(3.3.411) *koṭi* refers to extreme excellence; *jaṭā* is hair matted at the root.
(3.3.412) *vyuṣṭi* means fruit or prosperity; *dṛṣṭi* means knowledge, the eye, or seeing.
(3.3.413) *iṣṭi* is used in the sense of sacrifice and desire; *sṛṣṭa* is used for what is determined and for many things [in the plural];

(3.3.414) *kaṣṭa*, however, means hardship and impenetrability; *dakṣa* is used for skillful, slow, and free from disease; (3.3.415) *paṭu* has two meanings and is of common gender (*vācyaliṅga*); and *nīlakaṇṭha* refers also to Śiva.

(3.3.416) *poṭā* means a female slave; *dviliṅga* means both genders. (3.3.417) *ghṛṣṭī* refers to rubbing and a boar. (3.3.418) *ghaṭā* refers to a herd of cows, a troop of elephants, and a multitude; *kṛpīṭa* refers to the belly and water.
Thus end the words ending in *ṭ*.
(3.3.419) *Koṣṭha* is masculine; it denotes the interior of the belly (*antarjaṭhara*), a granary (*kusūla*), and likewise the interior of a house (*antargṛha*).
(3.3.420) *Niṣṭhā* signifies completion, destruction, and the end; *kāṣṭhā* is used for excellence, a fixed position, and a direction.
(3.3.421) *Jyeṣṭha* is used in three genders; it means most excellent as well as eldest; *kaniṣṭha* means youngest and also small.
(3.3.422) Thus end the words ending in *ṭha*.
(3.3.423) *Daṇḍa* may also refer to a staff (*laguḍa*) and is not exclusively masculine; *guḍa* refers to a ball and to the boiled juice of sugarcane.
(3.3.424) *Vyāḍa* refers to a serpent and to a beast of prey; *iḍā* and *ilā* refer to a cow, the earth, and speech.
(3.3.425) *Kṣveḍa* refers to a bamboo splinter or a tube, even when [measuring] six *kṣaṇas* in time;

(3.3.426) *kāṇḍa*, which is not feminine, denotes a staff, an arrow, a section of a plant, a group, an opportunity, and water; (3.3.427) *bhāṇḍa* may mean a horse's ornament, a vessel, or the capital of a merchant.
(3.3.428) Thus end the words ending in -ḍa.
(3.3.429) *Bāḍham* is used for "intense" (*bhṛśa*) and "firm promise" (*pratijñā*); *pragāḍham* is used for "intense" (*bhṛśa*) and "extreme difficulty" (*kṛcchra*).
(3.3.430) *Piṇḍī* is used for "a mass" (*saṃghāta*) and "swallowing" (*grāsa*); it is feminine in these two senses, but masculine when referring to a body (*kalevara*).
(3.3.431) *Gaṇḍa* refers to the cheeks or swellings on the temples; *muṇḍaka* is used in three genders for one who has been shorn.
(3.3.432) *Khaṇḍa* is not feminine and denotes a variety of sugarcane; *śikhaṇḍa* refers to a peacock’s tail-feather or a crest.
(3.3.433) *Dṛḍha* and *vyūḍha* are used in three genders for "firm" or "strong," while they also mean "arranged" or "drawn up in array" and "compact" or "heaped together."
(3.3.434) Thus end those ending in *ḍha*.
(3.3.435) *Bhrūṇa* refers to a child or the embryo of a woman; *bāṇa* refers to the son of Bali or an arrow.
(3.3.436) *Kaṇa* refers to something extremely minute or a particle of grain; *gaṇa* refers to a collection or a troop of attendants.
(3.3.437) *Paṇa* refers to a stake in gambling and the like, as well as wages, price, and wealth;
(3.3.438) *Guṇa* refers to a bowstring, as well as qualities inherent in substances such as courage, friendship, and so forth;
(3.3.439) *Kṣaṇa* refers to remaining inactive, a specific point of time, and a festival.
(3.3.440) *Varṇa* refers to the twice-born [castes] and so forth, as well as white and other colors; however, *varṇam* denotes praise or a syllable.
(3.3.441) *Aruṇa* may refer to the sun, and it is used in three genders for a particular color.
(3.3.442) *Sthāṇu* is Śiva; furthermore, *droṇa* refers to a crow, and *raṇa* denotes battle or sound.
(3.3.443) *Grāmaṇī* refers to a barber in the masculine, and to an excellent person or the head of a village in the three genders.
(3.3.444) *Ūrṇā* denotes the wool of sheep and the like, as well as the tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
(3.3.445) *Hariṇī* may be a female deer, a golden image, or that which is green.

(3.3.446) *Hariṇa* means "pale" in three genders; *sthūṇā* refers to the pillar of a house as well. (3.3.447) *Tṛṣṇā* denotes both longing and thirst; *ghṛṇā* signifies both loathing and compassion. (3.3.448) *Vipaṇi* refers to a marketplace; *vāruṇī* means both wine and the western quarter.
(3.3.449) *Kareṇu* and *ibha* denote a female and male elephant respectively; *draviṇa* means strength and wealth.
(3.3.450) *Śaraṇa* refers to a house and a protector; *śrīparṇa* also denotes the lotus.
(3.3.451) *Tīkṣṇa* is used in the neuter for poison, a sword, and iron; in the masculine it means sharp.
(3.3.452) *Pramāṇa* [is used] in the senses of cause, limit, scripture, measure, and the knower;
(3.3.453) *karaṇa* [is used] for the most effective instrument, as well as for field, limb, and sense organ;
(3.3.454) *saṃsaraṇa* [is used] for the birth of living beings and for the movement of an unobstructed army.
(3.3.455) *Ghaṇṭāpatha* refers to a main road; *samudgiraṇa* means vomiting or ejecting.
(3.3.456) From this point on, *viṣāṇa* is used in three genders: it denotes the horn of an animal and the tusk of an elephant.
(3.3.457) *Pravaṇa* refers to a sloping or gradually descending ground; as a masculine noun, however, it means a crossroads.
(3.3.458) *saṃkīrṇa* means mixed; *nicita* and *aśuddha* mean impure; *viriṇa*, *śūnya*, and *ūṣara* mean barren land.
(3.3.459) *caraṇa* refers to a bridge and a braid of hair; *veṇī* refers to a type of river and a mass of hair.
(3.3.460) Thus end the words ending in *ṇ*.
(3.3.461) *devasūryau* and *vivasvantau*, *sarasvantau* and *nadārṇavau*; (3.3.462) *pakṣitārkṣyau* and *garutmantau*, *śakuntau* and *bhāsapakṣiṇau*;
(3.3.463) *agnyutpātau* and *dhūmaketū*, *jīmūtau* and *meghaparvatau*.
(3.3.464) *hasta* refers to the hands, the asterism [Hasta], Maruta, and the wind-god;

(3.3.465) *yantṛ* refers to an elephant-driver and a charioteer; *bhartṛ* refers to a creator and a nourisher; (3.3.466) *pota* refers to a vessel and an infant; *preta* refers to a deceased being and one who has died.

(3.3.467) *Ketu* refers to a type of planet or a banner; (3.3.468) *suta* means a son or a prince; (3.3.468–469) *sthapati* denotes a master builder or a chief artisan; *bhūbhṛt* signifies a mountain or a king;
(3.3.469) *mūrdhābhiṣikta* refers to a consecrated monarch; and *ṛtu* means a woman or a flower.
(3.3.470) *Viṣṇu* also [is called] *Ajita* and *Avyakta*; *Sūta* refers to Tvaṣṭṛ and a charioteer;
(3.3.471) *Vyakta* is seen also in the sense of a wise man; both are examples found in the scriptures.
(3.3.472) *Kṣattṛ* may mean a charioteer, a doorkeeper, or one born of a Kṣatriya woman from a Śūdra father.

(3.3.473) *Vṛttānta* may mean a context, a manner, or the entirety of a report; (3.3.474) *Ānarta* refers to a battle, a place of dance, or a specific region; (3.3.475) *Kṛtānta* denotes Yama, a final conclusion, destiny, or an unwholesome action.
(3.3.476) Phlegm and so forth, the vital fluids such as plasma and blood, the great elements, and their qualities;
(3.3.477) the sense organs, modifications of stone, and the mineral ores which are the source of sound;
(3.3.478) even within the inner apartments, the "pure interior" (*śuddhānta*) of a king is not accessible to everyone.
(3.3.479) *Kāsū* [is used] in the senses of "a javelin" and "capacity"; *śakti* [is used] in the senses of "power" and "prowess"; and *mūrti* [is used] in the senses of "solidity" and "body."
(3.3.480) *Vratati* denotes both "creeper" and "extension"; *vasati* denotes both "night" and "dwelling.
(3.3.481) *Apaciti* denotes both "decay" and "honor"; *sāti* denotes both "giving" and "termination."

(3.3.482) *Ārti* means pain or affliction; it also refers to the tip of a bow. *Jāti* means a genus or species, as well as birth. (3.3.483) *Rīti* means movement or flow, as well as a style of composition. *Īti* means a riot or tumult, as well as an epidemic or calamity. (3.3.484) *Prāpti* means rising or emergence, as well as attainment. *Tretā*, however, refers to the triad of sacred fires, as well as the second of the four ages (*yuga*).
(3.3.485) *Mahatī* refers to a specific type of lute; it also means prosperity or ashes.
(3.3.486) *Bhogavatī* refers to a river or a city of the *nāgas*. (3.3.487) *Samiti* refers to battle, union, or an assembly; *kṣiti* refers to both destruction and the earth.
(3.3.488) *Ravi* means the sun; *arci*, a weapon, and the flame of fire; *hetayaḥ* means missiles.
(3.3.489) *Jagatī* refers to a specific meter as well as the earth.
(3.3.490) *Paṅkti* is also a meter, specifically the tenth; *āyati* refers to influence as well as the future.
(3.3.491) *Patti* means a foot-soldier or a step; *pakṣati* refers to the root of a tree or the division of a wing.
(3.3.492) *Prakṛti* denotes the womb or a grammatical base; it also refers to the dramatic styles (*vṛttis*) such as *kaiśikī*.
(3.3.493) *Sikatā* means sand; *śruti* is used for the Veda and for the ear.
(3.3.494) *Vanitā* refers to a woman who has produced excessive passion; (3.3.495) *Guptiḥ* means protection, as well as the clearing away of land; *Dhṛtiḥ* denotes maintenance and fortitude;
(3.3.496) *Bṛhatī* refers to the small eggplant (*vārtākī*), a specific type of meter, and also the great.
(3.3.497) *Vāsitā* refers to a female elephant and a woman; *vārtā* refers to livelihood, news, or rumor.
(3.3.498) *Vārta* means healthy or prosperous; it is used in three genders for water, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and nectar (*amṛta*).
(3.3.499) *Kaladhauta* refers to silver and gold; *nimitta* refers to a cause or a mark.
(3.3.500) *Śruta* is used for what has been heard from scripture and for that which is ascertained; *kṛta* is used for a pair, a sufficient amount, and what has been done.
(3.3.501) *Atyāhita* denotes great fear and an action that disregards one's life.
(3.3.502) *Bhūta* is used in the sense of "proper" when applied to the earth and so forth, and in the sense of "covered"; it is used in three genders to mean a living being and what has passed away.
(3.3.503) *Vṛtta* refers to a verse or conduct; it is used in three genders for what is past, firm, or flat.

(3.3.504) *Mahat* refers to a great kingdom; *avagīta* is used in the sense of "born" (*janye*) and in three genders for what is censured. (3.3.505) *Śveta* refers to silver; *rajata* refers to gold, silver, or white; [it is used] in three genders.
(3.3.506) The word *rakta* is used in three senses: as dyed with indigo and the like, as passionate, and as a mark;
(3.3.507) *avadāta* means white, yellow, and pure; *baddha* and *arjuna* mean white; (3.3.508) *abhinīta* means fit, highly refined, and patient; furthermore, *saṃskṛta* [is used in these senses].

(3.3.509) *Ananta* refers to both that which is artificial and that which possesses characteristics; it also means "without end" (*anavadhi*). (3.3.510) *Khyāta* means famous; *hṛṣṭa* means joyful; *pratīta* means understood; *abhijāta* means one born of noble lineage and also wise.
(3.3.511) *Vivikta* means pure and solitary; *mūrchita* means stupefied and also increased.
(3.3.512) *Śukta* means two things: sour and harsh; *śiti* means white and black.
(3.3.513) *Sat* is used in the sense of truth, what is good, existence, praise, and that which is worthy of honor.
(3.3.514) *Puraskṛta* refers to one who is honored, one who is attacked by an enemy, and one who is placed in front.
(3.3.515) *Nivāta* refers to a windless place; *āśraya* and *vāta* refer to a sheltered wind; and *varma* refers to armor that cannot be pierced by weapons.
(3.3.516) *Jāta*, *unnaddha*, and *pravṛddha* denote things that are elevated or risen; whereas these [following terms] denote things that have grown:
*vṛddhimat*, *praudya*, and *utpanna*. *Ādṛta* means attended with respect or honored.
(3.3.518) *jāta* and *mahijit* denote a collection; *śrīpati* and *indrapati* denote the husband [of Śrī and Indrāṇī].
(3.3.519) Even in the sense of "falling asleep," there is *prapāta*; furthermore, *avapāta*, *avataṭa*, and *avaṭa* [denote a precipice or pit].
(3.3.520) *Samit* denotes a gathering and also battle; *sthiti* is feminine and also denotes a fixed rule or state.
(3.3.521) *Artha* means that which is denoted (*abhidheya*), wealth (*rai*), a thing (*vastu*), purpose (*prayojana*), and cessation (*nivṛtti*).
(3.3.522) *Tīrtha* refers to a watering place (*nipāna*) and a sacred tradition (*āgama*); it also denotes water frequented by sages (*ṛṣijuṣṭa*) and a spiritual preceptor (*guru*).
(3.3.523) *Samartha* is used in three senses: being capable (*śaktistha*), having a connected meaning (*saṃbaddhārtha*), and being beneficial (*hita*).
(3.3.524) *Daśamīstha* refers to one whose passion is exhausted (*kṣīṇarāga*) or one who is aged (*vṛddha*); it also denotes a street (*vīthī*) or a path (*padavī*).
(3.3.525) *Āsthānī* means an assembly hall; *āsthā* means effort (*yatna*); *prastha* is not feminine and denotes a mountain ridge (*sānu*) or a measure of capacity (*māna*).
(3.3.526) *Grantha* refers to a treatise (*śāstra*) or wealth (*draviṇa*); *saṃsthā* refers to a support (*ādhāra*), a state of being established (*sthitau*), or death (*mṛtau*).
(3.3.527) Thus end those ending in *tha*.
(3.3.528) *Chandaḥ* and *abdaḥ* mean intention and year, like *jīmūtaḥ* [meaning cloud and year].
(3.3.529) But *apavādaḥ* means censure and knowledge; *dāyādaḥ* means son and kinsman.

(3.3.530) *Pāda* means a ray, a foot, a fourth part, and [the gods] Moon, Fire, and Sun, who dispel darkness; (3.3.531) *Nirvāda* refers to public rumor as well as censure; *śāda* refers to both mud and young grass; (3.3.532) *Ākranda* refers to crying out, a protector, and a fierce battle.
(3.3.533) *Prasāda* may mean favor or clarity; *sūda* may mean a cook or a sauce.
(3.3.534) *Govinda* may mean a superintendent of cattle or Viṣṇu; *mada* may mean joy or intoxication.
(3.3.535) *Kakuda*—which is not feminine—denotes preeminence, a royal insignia, or the hump on the shoulder of a bull.
(3.3.536) *strī* is used for woman, consciousness, knowledge, conversation, agreement, and names;
(3.3.537) *upaniṣad* is used for dharma and secret doctrine; *śarat* is used for season and year;
(3.3.538) *pada* is used for determination, protection, place, mark, foot, and object.
(3.3.539) *Goṣpada* [is used] in the sense of "frequented" and "measure"; *pratiṣṭhā*, *kṛtya*, and *āspada* mean "foundation.
(3.3.540) *Iṣṭa*, *madhura*, and *svādu* are three [words for] "sweet"; *mṛdu* means both "not sharp" and "tender.
(3.3.541) *Mūḍha*, *alpa*, *apaṭu*, and *nirbhāgya* are synonyms for "dull-witted"; furthermore, two [words], *śārada*, are [used for] "autumnal."

(3.3.542) *pratyagra* and *apratibha* mean "learned"; *supragalbha* and *viśārada* mean "confident. (3.3.543) These end with the letter *d*. (3.3.544) *Vyāma*, *vaṭa*, and *nyagrodha* mean "the span [of the arms]"; *utsedha*, *kāya*, and *unnati* mean "height" or "elevation."

(3.3.545) *paryāhāra* means a path; (3.3.546) *h* [is substituted for *vī*] in *vivadha* and *vīvadha*, both of which denote a pole for carrying loads; *paridhi* refers to the branch of a sacrificial tree or to the halo around the sun.
(3.3.547) *Bandhaka* is a calamity; *ādhi*s are the bases of mental affliction.
(3.3.548) *Samarthana*, *nīvāka*, and *niyama* are synonyms for *samādhi*.
(3.3.549) *Anubandha* refers to the production of a fault; it occurs when that which is begun perishes at its inception.
(3.3.550) *Mukhya* refers to a child who follows his elders by nature;
(3.3.551) *vidhu* means Viṣṇu, the moon, separation, or a hole; (3.3.552) *vidhi* means an ordinance or fate; *praṇidhi* means a request or a spy.

(3.3.553) *Budha* means "to grow" and also refers to a "learned man"; *skandha* means "a collection" and also [the trunk of a tree]. (3.3.554) *Sindhu* is masculine when it means "a country," "a specific river," or "the ocean," and feminine when it means "a river.
(3.3.555) *Vidhā* means "fate," "manner," and "kind"; *sādhu* means "excellent" and also "beautiful," used in three genders.

(3.3.556) *Vadhū* means a wife, a daughter-in-law, or a woman; *sudhā* means plastering or nectar; *snuhī* [means the Euphorbia plant]. (3.3.557) *Sandhā* means a promise, a boundary, faith, or longing. (3.3.558) *Madhu* refers to wine, the juice of flowers, or honey; it also refers to blinding darkness.
(3.3.559) From *atas*, in three senses: *samunnaddha* means "learned" (*paṇḍita*), "conceited" (*manya*), and "proud" (*garvita*).
(3.3.560) *Brahmabandhu* is used in the sense of "insulting"; furthermore, *avalambita* is used in the sense of "indicating.
(3.3.561) *Avidūra* also [means] "near" (*avaṣṭabdha*); *khyāta* and *bhūṣita* are used in the sense of "famous" (*prasiddhi*).
(3.3.562) *gandha* [is used] in the sense of a trace (*leśa*); (3.3.563) *saṃbādha* [is used] in the sense of a crowded place (*guhya*) and a dense mass (*saṃkula*);
*bādhā* [is used] in the sense of obstruction (*niṣedha*) and suffering (*duḥkha*). *Jñātṛ*, *cāndri*, and *sura* are [names for] the wise (*budha*).
Thus end those [roots] ending in *dh*.
(3.3.564) *Sūrya* and *vahni* are synonyms for the sun; *citrabhānu* and *bhānu* refer to the sun and its rays; *divākara* means the maker of day.
(3.3.565) *Bhūtātman* and *dhātṛ* refer to the soul and the body; *mūrkha* and *nīca* refer to fools and base persons; *pṛthagjana* refers to common people.
(3.3.566) *Grāvan* and *śaila* refer to mountains and stones; *patrin* refers to arrows and birds.

(3.3.567) *taru* and *śaila* are both *śikhariṇau*; *śikhin* refers to fire and a peacock; (3.3.568) both *pratiyatna* refer to desire for gain and protection; furthermore, *sādin* refers to two things: a charioteer and a horseman; (3.3.569) *vājinaḥ* refers to horses and birds.

(3.3.570) *Abhijana* refers to lineage or birth, and also to native land; furthermore, *hāyana* refers to years, (3.3.571) the rainy season, flames, varieties of rice, the moon, fire, the sun, and the sun-god Virocana;
(3.3.572) *vṛjina* refers to hair as well as sin; and *viśvakarman* refers to both the sun and the divine architect.
(3.3.573) *Ātman* means effort, fortitude, intellect, inherent nature, the Veda, and the body;
(3.3.574) *Śakra* means Indra, a killer, a rutting elephant, a rain-cloud, and a thundercloud (*ghanāghana*);
(3.3.575) *Abhimāna* refers to pride regarding wealth and the like, as well as knowledge, affection, and injury.
(3.3.576) *Ghana* refers to a cloud, a quality of form, or, as a tri-lingual term, something solid or dense; (3.3.577) *ina* means the sun or a lord; *rājā* means the moon, a kṣatriya, or a king;
(3.3.578) *vāṇinī* refers to a dancer or a female messenger; and *vāhinī* also refers to a flowing river.
(3.3.579) *hlādinī* refers to lightning and the thunderbolt; it also denotes a woman who desires [her husband].
(3.3.580) *tanu* refers to both skin and the body; it also means a sacrificial altar and the tongue.
(3.3.581) *vitāna*, which is not feminine, refers to a sacrifice and a canopy; in three genders, it means something trifling.
(3.3.582) Furthermore, *ketanam* is used in the sense of "sluggishness," as well as for "a rite to be performed" (*kṛtya*), "a banner" (*ketu*), and "an invitation.
(3.3.583) *Veda*, *tattva*, *tapas*, *brahma*, *brahmā*, *vipra*, and *prajāpati* [are synonyms for the Veda].
(3.3.584) *Gandhanam* is used in the sense of "encouraging," "injuring," and also "hinting."
(3.3.585) *Ātañcana* means coagulating, adding an ingredient, speeding up, or nourishing;
(3.3.586) *vyañjana* means a mark, a sign, a beard, or even a condiment; (3.3.587) *kaulīna* occurs in the sense of public rumor, battle, or [the breeding] of cattle and birds.
(3.3.588) *Udyāna* may mean departure, a type of forest, or a purpose;
(3.3.589) *sthāna* means an open space or a state of standing; *devana* refers to play and so forth; (3.3.590) *vyutthāna* means obstruction as well as the practice of opposition.
(3.3.591) *Sādhana* [is used] in the sense of exertion (*utthāna*) in the context of human effort (*pauruṣa-tantra*), as well as in the sense of origin (*saṃniviṣṭodgama*).

(3.3.592) It is also used in the sense of killing (*māraṇa*), the funeral rites for the deceased (*mṛtasaṃskāra*), going (*gati*), wealth (*dravya*), purpose (*artha*), causing to give (*dāpana*), accomplishment (*nirvartana*), implements (*upakaraṇa*), and following (*anuvrajyā*). (3.3.593) [In these cases, it is used] as the means (*sādhana*).
(3.3.594) *Niryātana* means the clearing of enmity, giving, or the restoration of a deposit;
(3.3.595) *vyasana* refers to misfortune, ruin, vice, or that which arises from passion or anger;
(3.3.596) *pakṣman* denotes the eyelashes, the filaments of a flower, or even the finest thread-like part.
(3.3.597) *Parvan* means a division of lunar days (*tithi*), a moment (*kṣaṇa*), a festival (*parva*), a path (*vartman*), or the eyelid (*netracchada*).
(3.3.598) *Kaupīna* refers to a shameful act (*akārya*) or a private part; *maithuna* means union (*saṃgati*) or sexual intercourse (*rata*).
(3.3.599) *Pradhāna* means the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or the intellect (*dhī*); *prajñāna* means wisdom (*prajñā*) or a mark of intelligence (*buddhicihna*).
(3.3.600) *Prasūnam* refers to both a flower and fruit; *nidhanam* refers to both death and the destruction of a lineage.
(3.3.601) *Krandanam* refers to weeping and calling out; *varṣma* refers to both the body and height.
(3.3.602) *Dhāma* refers to a house, the body, splendor, and power; furthermore, it denotes a crossroads.
(3.3.603) *Saṃniveśa* means arrangement; *saṃsthāna* means a mark, a characteristic, or that which is predominant.
(3.3.604) Both *saṃvidhāna* and *apavāraṇa* mean covering.
(3.3.605) *Ārādhana* may mean accomplishment, attainment, or even pleasing.
(3.3.606) *Adhiṣṭhānam* is used in the senses of a wheel, a city, influence, and sitting;

(3.3.607) *ratnam* is used for the best of its kind, as well as for a forest, water, and a grove; (3.3.608) *talinam* means sparse or small, and it is of common gender (applicable to all genders), as are the following terms.
(3.3.609) *samānaḥ*, *sat*, and *sama* mean "equal"; *piśunaḥ* and *sūcakaḥ* mean "a malicious informer" or "a backbiter.
(3.3.610) *hīnaḥ*, *nyūnaḥ*, *ūnaḥ*, and *garhyaḥ* mean "inferior" or "blameworthy"; *vegin* and *śūraḥ* mean "swift" or "valiant.
(3.3.611) *abhipannaḥ* means "one who has offended," "one who is seized," or "one who has fallen into calamity."
Thus end those ending in -n (3.3.612).
*Kalāpa* means an ornament, a peacock’s tail-feather, a quiver, and also a collection (3.3.613). *Parīvāpa* means a surrounding enclosure, scattering, and standing in water.
(3.3.614) *godhuk* and *goṣṭhapati* denote two types of cowherds; *hari* and *viṣṇu* denote the two [forms of] Śiva; *vṛṣākapī* denotes the two [forms of] Viṣṇu.
(3.3.615) *bāṣpa*, *ūṣman*, and *aśru* denote tears; *kaśipu* denotes both food and clothing.
(3.3.616) *talpa* refers to a bed, a palace, or a wife; *viṭapa* (masculine/neuter) refers to a tree trunk or a branch.
(3.3.617) *Prāptarūpa*, *svarūpa*, and *abhirūpa* [are used] for one who is wise or pleasing to the mind.
(3.3.618) These [words] have genders according to the object they qualify (*bhedyaliṅga*); *kūrmī* is a type of lute, and *kacchapī* is also a type of lute.
(3.3.619) *Kutapa* refers to a cloth made from animal hair and also to the eighth part of a day.
Thus ends [the section on] words ending in *pānta* (3.3.620).
*Śiphā* refers to a lock of hair, a river, and the mother of Māṃsikā (3.3.621).
*Śapha* denotes the root of trees and also the hoof of cattle and other such animals.

(3.3.622) *Gulpha* refers to the ankle; it is also celebrated as a decoration for the arm. (3.3.623) *Repha* occurs in the masculine when denoting the letter *ra*; it is of common gender (*vācyaliṅgaka*) when signifying something contemptible. Thus end those words ending in *pha*.
(3.3.624) *Antarābhava-sattva* refers to an intermediate state being; *gandharva* refers to a celestial musician.
(3.3.625) *Kambu* refers to a bracelet or a conch shell; *dvijihva* refers to a serpent or a slanderer.
(3.3.626) The word *pūrva*, which possesses other genders, is used in the masculine plural to denote ancestors.

(3.3.627) *citrapuṅkha* also [means] a *kādamba* (a kind of goose); *nitamba* [means] a mountain slope and a hip; (3.3.628) *darvī* also [means] a hood; *bimba* is not feminine and also [means] a circle.
Thus end those ending in *ba*.
(3.3.629) *Kumbhau* refers to two jars, the frontal globes of an elephant, or the two parts of a head; *ḍimbhau*, however, denotes a child and a fool.
(3.3.630) *Stambhau* signifies a pillar and the state of being dull-witted; *śambhū* refers to Brahmā and the Three-eyed One (Śiva).
(3.3.631) *Garbhāḥ* denotes the belly, an embryo, and a child; *visrambhaḥ* refers to confidence as well as affection.

(3.3.632) *Dundubhi* may be used for a kettle-drum (*bherī*) as a masculine noun; it may also be used for a die (*akṣa*) as a feminine noun. (3.3.633) *Kusumbha* is neuter when referring to saffron (*mahārajata*); it is masculine when referring to a water-jar (*karaka*). (3.3.634) *Nābhi* is also used for a Kṣatriya as a masculine noun; *surabhi* is used for a cow (*go*) as a feminine noun.

(3.3.635) *Sabhā* refers to an assembly (*saṃsad*) and a member of that assembly (*sabhyā*); it is used in three genders. *Vallabha* also refers to a supervisor (*adhyakṣa*). These are the words ending in *bh*. (3.3.636) *Kiraṇa* and *pragraha* mean rays; *plavaṅgama* means both a monkey and a frog.
(3.3.637) *Icchā* and *manobhava* are synonyms for *kāma*; *śakti* and *udyoga* are synonyms for *parākrama*.
(3.3.638) *Dharma* refers to merit (*puṇya*), justice (*nyāya*), inherent nature (*svabhāva*), conduct (*ācāra*), and the Soma-drinkers (*somapa*).
(3.3.639) An undertaking preceded by a means is called *upadhā* as well as *upakrama*.

(3.3.640) *vaṇikpathaḥ*, *puraṃ*, *vedaḥ*, *nigamaḥ*, *nāgaraḥ*, and *vaṇik* [are synonyms for merchant/trade]. (3.3.641) *naigamaḥ* refers to two [things]: a merchant and one of the two [types of] strength (*bala*). *Rāmaḥ* [is used] in three genders when referring to the dark-blue, the beautiful, and the white. (3.3.642) *Grāmaḥ* [also denotes] a multitude preceded by words such as *śabda-*; *vikramaḥ* [denotes] prowess or stride.
(3.3.643) *Stoma* means praise, a sacrifice, or a multitude; *jihvā* means crooked or lazy.
(3.3.644) *Gharma* also means heat; *vibhrama* means movement, ornament, or delusion.
(3.3.645) *Gulma* means disease, a pillar, or an army; *jāmi* refers to a sister or a female of the family.
(3.3.646) *Kṣamā* means the earth or forbearance; *kṣama* is used in three genders to mean fit, capable, or beneficial.
(3.3.647) In three genders, *śyāma* means green or black; *śyāmā* refers to the *śārivā* plant or the night.
(3.3.648) *Lalāma* refers to a tail, a mark on the forehead, a horse, an ornament, preeminence, or a banner.

(3.3.649) *Sūkṣma* means subtle; *madhyātman* refers to the first [of the three guṇas] in the primary sense; and *prathama* occurs in three senses. (3.3.650) *Vāma* has two meanings: beautiful and adverse; *adhama* means inferior and contemptible.
(3.3.651) *Jīrṇa* and *paribhukta*—these two denote that which is worn out or used up; this term is *yātayāma*.
Thus ends the section on words ending in *gān* (3.3.652).
*Turaṅga* and *garuḍa* are both *tārkṣya*; *nilaya* and *apacaya* are both *kṣaya*; *devara* and *śyāla* are both *śvaśurya*; and *bhrātṛja* and *dviṣ* are both *bhrātṛvya*.
(3.3.654) *Parjanya* refers to Indra and the rain-god; *arya* denotes a master and a Vaiśya.
(3.3.655) *Tiṣya* refers to the Puṣya constellation and the Kali age; *paryāya* means opportunity and sequence.
(3.3.656) *Pratyaya* occurs in the senses of dependence, oath, knowledge, trust, and cause.

(3.3.657) *Randhra* means a hole or an opening, as well as a sound; *anuśaya* means long-standing enmity or remorse. (3.3.658) *Sthūloccaya* means incompleteness or deficiency, as well as the middle pace of elephants. (3.3.659) *Samaya* refers to an oath, custom, time, established doctrine, or an agreement.
(3.3.660) *Vyasana*, *aśubha*, *daiva*, *vipad*, and *anaya*—these three [terms] are synonyms for misfortune.
(3.3.661) *Atyaya* is used in the sense of transgression, hardship, fault, punishment, and also in the sense of calamity (*āpad*).
(3.3.662) *Saṃparāya* refers to battle and the future; furthermore, it denotes one who is venerable and also a father-in-law (*śvaśura*).
(3.3.663) *Sannaya* refers to a force stationed in the rear and a military array;
(3.3.664) *saṃstyāya* denotes a gathering and a settlement; and these *praṇayas* (3.3.665) signify confidence, a request, and affection, while *samucchraya* also denotes hostility.

(3.3.666) That whose object is known is its *viṣaya*; (3.3.667) *kaṣāya* refers to an extract, and is also feminine; *pratiśraya* means an assembly hall or a shelter; (3.3.668) *prāyaḥ* signifies abundance or departure; *manyuḥ* denotes dejection, a sacrifice, or anger.

(3.3.669) *Guhyam* is used for "secret" and "the private parts"; *satyam* is used for "an oath" and "truth. (3.3.670) *Vīryam* is used for "strength" and "prowess"; *dravyam* is used for "that which is fit" and "the substratum of qualities. (3.3.671) *Dhiṣṇyam* is used for "place," "house," "asterism," and "fire"; *bhāgyam* is used for "destiny" and "auspicious or inauspicious action."

(3.3.672) Kaśeru, heman, gāṅgeya, viśalyā, and also dantikā; (3.3.673) vṛṣākapāyī is a designation for Śrī and Gaurī, as well as for recognition and beauty; (3.3.674) ārambha, niṣkṛti, śikṣā, pūjana, and saṃpradhāraṇa.
(3.3.675) *Upāya* means means, action, effort, and medical treatment; there are nine types of actions.
(3.3.676) *Chāyā* means the beloved of the sun, luster, a reflection, and non-sunlight.
(3.3.677) *Kakṣyā* refers to the inner courtyard of a palace and the like, a girdle, and the middle part of an elephant’s neck where it is bound.
(3.3.678) *Kṛtya* refers to a grammatical suffix denoting action or a deity; it is used in three genders when something is to be divided by means of wealth and so forth.
(3.3.679) *Janya* may mean a public rumor; *jaghanya* refers to the last-born, as well as that which is base or inferior.
(3.3.680) *Garhya* and *adhīna* are to be stated [as synonyms]; *kalya* means healthy, as well as a virtuous person.
(3.3.681) *Ātmavān* means one who does not deviate from the goal; *arthya* means meritorious, while *cāru* also means beautiful.

(3.3.682) *Rūpya* refers to that which has a praiseworthy form, while *vadānya* refers to one who speaks elegantly. (3.3.683) *Madhya* refers to what is just, while *saumya* refers to what is beautiful or presided over by the deity Soma.
Thus end those ending in -yā (3.3.684): *nivaha*, *avasara*, *vāra*, *saṃstara*, *prastara*, *adhvara* (3.3.685);
*guru* refers to the teacher, the father of the earth (*goṣpati*), the father, and so forth; *dvāpara* refers to an age (*yuga*) and doubt (*saṃśaya*).
(3.3.686) *Prakāra* means variety (*bheda*) or similarity (*sādṛśya*); *ākāra* means gesture (*iṅgita*) or form (*ākṛti*).
(3.3.687) *Kiṃśāru* refers to the awn of grain; *maru* refers to a desert (*dhanva*) or a mountain (*dharādhara*).
(3.3.688) *Adri* refers to a tree, a mountain, or the sun; *payodhara* refers to a woman’s breast or a cloud.
(3.3.689) *Dhvānta*, *ari*, and *dānava* denote darkness; *vṛtra* denotes an enemy; *bali*, *hasta*, *aṃśu*, and *kara* denote taxes or rays;

(3.3.690) *pradara*, *bhanga*, *nārīruka*, *bāṇa*, *asra*, and *kaca* denote hair; (3.3.691) a bull that has not yet grown horns and a man who is still beardless at his proper age are both called *tūbara*.
(3.3.692) *Rāḥ* also means gold; *parikara* refers to a retinue or a bed-cover.
(3.3.693) *Tāra* occurs in the sense of purity of pearls; *śāra*, however, means wind, and it is used in three genders [for a variegated object].
(3.3.694) Furthermore, *saṃgara* denotes a promise, a battle, an agreement, and a calamity.
(3.3.695) *Mantra* refers to a division of the Vedas or secret counsel; *mitra* means the sun as well.
(3.3.696) *Svaru* refers to a fragment of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) used in sacrifices; *avaskara* also refers to that which is secret.
(3.3.697) *Āḍambara* refers to the sound of musical instruments and the trumpeting of lordly elephants.

(3.3.698) *Abhihāra* means an attack, as well as theft and the act of arming oneself for battle; (3.3.699) *parīvāra* refers to that which moves, the scabbard of a sword, and personal attendants; (3.3.700) *viṣṭara* denotes a tree, a handful of *darbha* grass, and a seat such as a stool.
(3.3.701) *Dvāri* means at the door; *pratīhāraḥ* and *pratīhārī* mean a doorkeeper (in the latter case, also feminine).
(3.3.702) *Babhruḥ* refers to a large mongoose, to Viṣṇu, and as an adjective (*triṣu*), it means tawny.
(3.3.703) *Sāraḥ* means strength, the solid core of something, and what is right or essential; as a neuter noun (*klībaṃ*) it has these meanings, while as an adjective (*triṣu*) it means excellent.
(3.3.704) *durodara* refers to a gambler, while *durodara* also means the stake or the game of dice itself.

(3.3.705) *Kāntāra*—whether masculine or neuter—denotes a great forest or a difficult path. (3.3.706) *Matsara* signifies hatred of another's prosperity; when applied to one who possesses such [hatred] or to a miser, it is used in all three genders.
(3.3.707) *vara* following *deva* means "chosen" (*vṛta*); when meaning "excellent," it is used in three genders, but as a neuter it means "slightly dear.
(3.3.708) *Karīra* refers to a bamboo shoot; it is not feminine, but as a masculine it denotes a specific type of tree and a water jar.
(3.3.709) *Pratisara* is masculine and refers to the rear of an army; as a neuter it denotes a wrist-thread (*hastasūtra*).
(3.3.710) *Yama*, *anila*, *indra*, *candra*, *arka*, *viṣṇu*, *siṃha*, *aṃśu*, and *vājī*;
(3.3.711) *hari* is masculine when referring to a parrot, a snake, a monkey, or a frog; it is also used in the sense of "tawny" (*kapila*) in three genders.
(3.3.712) *Śarkarā* also refers to a fragment of a potsherd; *yātrā* may mean a journey or a march.
(3.3.713) *Irā* may mean earth, speech, wine, or water; *tandrī* means drowsiness or lassitude.
(3.3.714) *Dhātrī* may mean a foster-mother, the earth, or the *āmalaka* tree.
(3.3.715) *Kṣudrā* refers to a woman with missing limbs, an actress, a courtesan, a honeybee, or the *kaṇṭakārikā* plant.
(3.3.716) *Kṣudra* is used in three senses: cruel, base, and small; *mātrā* refers to a covering or garment.
(3.3.717) It also denotes a small measure; as a measure, *mātram* signifies entirety or restriction.
