(3.3.718) *Citra* refers to painting and wonder; *kalatra* refers to the hips and a wife.
(3.3.719) *pātra* or *patra* [is used] for a worthy person or a vessel, and for a vehicle or a wing;
(3.3.720) *śāstra* [is used] for an instruction or a book, and *śastra* for a weapon or iron;
(3.3.721) *netra* may refer to matted hair or a garment, and *kṣetra* to a wife or the body.
(3.3.722) *Potram* refers to the snout of a boar or a ploughshare; *gotram* refers to a name or lineage.
(3.3.723) *Satram* refers to a covering, a sacrifice, a constant gift, or even a forest. (3.3.724) *Ajiram* refers to a field or the body; *ambaram* refers to the sky or a garment.
(3.3.725) *Cakra* refers to a kingdom, while *akṣara* refers to both the imperishable and milk; *kṣīra* refers to milk and water.
(3.3.726) Both *bhūri* and *candra* refer to gold; *gopura* refers even to a mere gate.
(3.3.727) *Guhā* and *dambha* both mean a cave; *gahvara* means a secret place, a proximity, or a secluded spot.

(3.3.728) *puraḥ* means "in front," "additional," "above," or "at the beginning"; *puram* refers to a house or a city. (3.3.729) *mandiram* is also [a word for a palace]. Furthermore, *rāṣṭraḥ*—not feminine—is used for a kingdom or a calamity. (3.3.730) *daraḥ*—not feminine—is used for fear or a chasm; *vajraḥ*—not feminine—is used for a diamond or a thunderbolt.
(3.3.731) *Tantra* refers to a primary system, a final doctrine, weaving, or a section;
(3.3.732) *Auśīra* refers to a chowrie (*cāmara*), a staff, and also to a bed or seat;
(3.3.733) *Puṣkara* refers to the tip of an elephant’s trunk, the mouth of a musical instrument, and water.

(3.3.734) *Vyoman* means the sky, a sword-blade, a lotus, a sacred ford, and a specific medicinal herb; (3.3.735) *Antara* means space, limit, clothing, disappearance, difference, purpose, (3.3.736) a hole, one's own, absence, outside, opportunity, the middle, and the inner self.
(3.3.737) *piṭhara* also means a winnowing basket; (3.3.738) *nāgara* also refers to *rājakaśeruka* (a type of plant);

*śārvara* refers to blinding darkness; (3.3.739) *ghātuka* is an adjective whose gender varies according to the noun it qualifies; *gaura* means reddish-brown, white, or yellow; and *aruṣkara* also means a wound.

(3.3.740) *Jaṭhara* may also mean "hard" as well as "belly"; (3.3.741) *adhara* means "below" as well as "lower lip"; (3.3.742) *ekāgra* means "undisturbed" as well as "one-pointed," while *vyagra* means "busy" as well as "disturbed.
*Uttara* occurs in the sense of "higher," "northern," or "best," whereas *anuttara* [is its opposite].

(3.3.743) In the opposite sense of these [words], *para* means "best," "distant," "not-self," or "supreme" (3.3.744). *Madhura* means both "sweet" and "dear. *Krūra* means "cruel" and "hard-hearted. (3.3.745) *Udāra* means "munificent" and "great"; however, the other [meaning] is "different" and "lowly."

(3.3.746) *Svaira* means "slow" or "at one's own will"; *śubhra* means "bright" or "white. (3.3.747) *Āsāra* refers to a "heavy downpour," as well as the "advancing of an army. (3.3.748) It also denotes the "falling of a stream of water" and "excellence"; *kaṭāha*, however, means a "cauldron" or "skull."
(3.3.749) *Bandhura* means beautiful or bent; it refers to a mountain, the moon, and a rock.
(3.3.750) *Caru* refers to a cooking pot or the preparation of an oblation; *adhīra* means cowardly or fickle. These are the words ending in *r*.
(3.3.751) *Cūḍā*, *kirīṭa*, and bound hair—these three are synonyms for a crown.
(3.3.752) *Pīlava* refers to various types of trees, elephants, stalks, and flowers. (3.3.753) *Kāla* denotes both destiny and time; *kali* refers to the fourth age.
(3.3.754) *Kamala* may refer to a deer, and *kambala* to a cloak. (3.3.755) *Bali* is masculine when meaning a hand or an offering; it is feminine when derived from a limb of a living being.
(3.3.756) *Bala* is neuter when meaning stoutness, strength, or an army; it is masculine when referring to the crow or Śiśupāla.

(3.3.757) *Vātūla* refers to a whirlwind (*vātyā*) in the masculine, and to one who cannot endure the wind (*vātāsaha*) in the three genders; (3.3.758) *Vyāla* has variable gender when meaning "cunning" (*śaṭha*), and is masculine when meaning a beast of prey or a snake; (3.3.759) *Mala* is not feminine and denotes sin, excrement, or dregs; *Śūla* is not feminine and denotes pain or a weapon.

(3.3.760) *Śaṅku* means a peg or wedge; it refers to two things. *Pāli* is used for a ridge, a corner, a mark, and a row. (3.3.761) *Kalā* refers to an art or a division of time. *Ālī* and *avalī* both mean a friend or a row.
(3.3.762) *Velā* refers to the change of the ocean's waters, as well as time and a boundary.
(3.3.763) *Bahula* refers to the Kṛttikā stars, to cows, and to fire; it is used in three genders when meaning "much" or "cold.
(3.3.764) *Līlā* denotes sport and graceful movement; *upalā* refers to a pebble and also to sugar.
(3.3.765) *Kīlāla* means blood and water; *mūla* means the root, as well as the primary source, a fibrous root, and fear.

(3.3.766) *Jālam* means a collection, as well as a net, a window-lattice, and a sieve. (3.3.767) *Śīlam* refers to innate disposition (*svabhāva*) and virtuous conduct (*sadvṛtta*). (3.3.768) *Phalam* refers to a crop (*sasya*) and that which is produced by a cause (*hetukṛta*).
*Paṭalam* is neuter when meaning a covering (*chadiḥ*) or an eye disease (*netraruj*); it is not masculine when meaning a collection (*samūha*).
(3.3.769) *Talam* denotes that which is below or its own form, provided it is not feminine; *palam* means meat.
(3.3.770) *Pātālam* refers to the submarine fire (*aurvānala*) as well; *celam* means a garment, and [the word *adhama*] is used in three genders for what is base.
(3.3.771) *Kukūlam* refers to a pit strewn with spikes, but as a masculine noun, it denotes a fire of chaff.
(3.3.772) *Nirṇīta* means "ascertained"; *kevala* has three genders and means both "alone" and "entire.
(3.3.773) *Kuśala* is used in the sense of "sufficiency," "welfare," and "merit," while it has three genders when meaning "skilled.
(3.3.774) *Pravāla* refers to a sprout and is not feminine; it has three genders and also means "thick" or "dull."
*Karāla* refers to that which is jagged and high; *peśala* means clever and skillful; *bāla* may denote a fool or even a child; *lola* signifies both restless and thirsty;
*kula* refers to a house as well; and *ekakuṇḍala* denotes the Tālāṅka tree and Kubera.
(3.3.778) *Helā* denotes feminine nature and contempt; *heli* means the sun; *hili* means battle.
(3.3.779) *Hāla* refers to a king and liquor; *dala* means a fragment and a leaf.
(3.3.780) *Tūli* signifies a variegated object, a probe, and a bed of cotton.
(3.3.781) *Tumula* refers to a tumultuous noise; *śaṣkulī* also means the outer ear. These end in *l*.
(3.3.782) *Dava* and *dāva* refer to forest fires; *bhava* refers to birth and Śiva.

(3.3.783) *Mantrin* and *sahāya* mean minister; *pati*, *śākhin*, and *narā* mean husband; (3.3.784) *avayaḥ* means mountain, sheep, and sun; *ājñā*, *hvāna*, and *adhvara* mean command, calling, and sacrifice respectively; *havāḥ* means oblation; (3.3.785) *bhāvaḥ* refers to existence, inherent nature, intention, action, soul, and birth.

(3.3.786) *Prasava* occurs in the sense of production, fruit, or a flower; it also denotes the delivery of a fetus. (3.3.787) *Nihnava* is used for lack of trust, concealment, and also for deceit. (3.3.788) *Utsava* refers to arrogance, resentment, the expansion of desire, and a great festival.
(3.3.789) *Anubhāva* refers to power as well as the firm conviction of the minds of the virtuous;
(3.3.790) *prabhava* denotes the cause of birth and the place where something is first perceived;
(3.3.791) the son born of a Brahmin father and a Śūdra mother is considered a *pāraśava*.
(3.3.792) *Dhruva* is used in the masculine when meaning "non-deviation" (*bheda*); it is neuter when meaning "certainty," and in the three genders when meaning "eternal.
(3.3.793) *Sva* means "kinsman" or "self" in the masculine; in the three genders it means "one's own"; in the feminine it means "wealth.
(3.3.794) *Nīvī* refers to the knot of the waist-cloth, a stake in a wager, and also a deposit.
(3.3.795) *Śivā* refers to Gaurī and the jackal; *dvandva* refers to a pair, a quarrel, and a couple.
(3.3.796) *Sattva* refers to substances, effort, and courage; it is not feminine when referring to living beings.
(3.3.797) *Klība* means a eunuch or a neuter; it is used as a term for one lacking virility and has all genders when used as an adjective.
Thus, *vānta* (3.3.798);
*viśau* means a Vaiśya and a man; *cārābhimarau* and *spaśau* (3.3.799) both mean a spy;
*dvau rāśī* refers to a heap and the zodiac signs such as Aries; and *dvau vaṃśau* refer to a lineage and bamboo.
(3.3.800) *Rahaḥ* means privacy; *prakāśaḥ* means manifestation; *vīkāśaḥ* means space or opportunity; *nirveśaḥ* refers to both wages and enjoyment.
(3.3.801) *Kīnāśaḥ* is masculine when meaning the god of death (Yama); it is used in three genders when meaning a mean person or a small farmer.
(3.3.802) *Apadeśaḥ* may mean a word, a mark, or a cause; *kuśam* means water.
(3.3.803) *Daśā* may mean a state or condition, and it also has many other senses; *āśā* means hope or thirst, and it is also used for a long distance.
(3.3.804) *Vaśā* refers to a woman or a female elephant; *dṛk* is used in the sense of vision or knowledge, and in the three genders it denotes a knower.
(3.3.805) *Karkaśa* refers to one who acts with rashness, as well as being hard or unpolished.
(3.3.806) *Prakāśa* means light; *bāliśa* refers to one who is very young or a fool;

(3.3.807) *nāśa* means destruction or disappearance; *jīviteśa* refers to a beloved or Yama; (3.3.808) *nistriṃśa* refers to a cruel person or a sword; *aṃśu* refers to the sun, while *aṃśavaḥ* refers to rays or hands.
(3.3.809) *Āśu* denotes speed; *śālī* denotes rice; *śīghra* denotes swiftness; *pāśa* denotes a bond and a weapon. Thus end the words ending in *ś*.
(3.3.810) *Sura* and *matsya* denote gods and fish; *animiṣa* denotes gods; *puruṣa* denotes the Self (*ātman*) and a human being (*mānava*).
(3.3.811) *Kāka* and *matsya* denote two types of birds; *dhvāṅkṣa* denotes two types of trees; and *kakṣa* denotes grass and climbing plants.
(3.3.812) *Abhīpuḥ* refers to a rein used for holding fast; *praiṣaḥ* refers to sending forth and crushing.
(3.3.813) *Pakṣaḥ* also refers to an ally; *uṣṇīṣaḥ* refers to a turban and a crown.
(3.3.814) *Vṛṣa* refers to semen, a mouse, an excellent person, merit, and a bull;

(3.3.815) *Kośa*, which is not feminine, means a bud, the scabbard of a sword, a mass of wealth, and a divine object; (3.3.816) *Ākarṣa* refers to gambling, dice, and also a chessboard; furthermore, *akṣa* refers to a sense organ.
(3.3.817) [The suffix -aṇ is applied] after *dyūtāṅga* (an element of gambling), *karṣacakra* (the wheel of a plow), *vyavahāra* (legal proceeding), and *kalidruma* (the tree of the Kali age).
(3.3.818) *Karṣū* means a trench; *karīṣāgni* means a fire of dried cow-dung; *karṣa* denotes a small stream. (3.3.819) *Pauruṣa* refers to manhood, its action, poison, and water.
(3.3.820) *Āmiṣa* may mean "acquisition" as well as "offense"; (3.3.821) *kilbiṣa* means "sin. (3.3.822) *Varṣa*, which is not feminine, denotes rain, a portion of a world-system, or a year.
*Prekṣā* refers to the watching of a dance, wisdom, alms, service, a request for wealth, or wages.

(3.3.823) *tviṭ* means splendor; it is used in three genders when followed by another word. (3.3.824) *nyakṣam* means entirety or the lowest. (3.3.825) *adhyakṣaḥ* means before one's eyes or appointed; *rūkṣaḥ* means devoid of affection or unsmooth.
*Lakṣam* refers to a pretext, a number, or a target (*śaravya*). *Ghoṣau* refers to sound and a multitude.

(3.3.826) *Kapiśīrṣa* refers to a turret on a wall; (3.3.827) *anutarṣa* means a drinking vessel, and *surā* means liquor; (3.3.828) *doṣa* refers to wind and other humors [of the body], while *doṣā* refers to the night; *dakṣa* also refers to a cock;
*śuṇḍā* refers to the tip of the trunk; and *gaṇḍūṣa* is used in two genders for the filling of the mouth.
Thus end the words ending in -ṣa and -ta (3.3.829).
*Haṃsau* refers to the sun and the white-winged bird; *vibhāvasū* refers to the sun and fire (3.3.830).
*Vatsau* means both a calf and a yearling; and *sāraṅgau* refers to both deer and gods.
(3.3.831) *Rasa* refers to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, poison, potency, a quality, passion, and liquid.
(3.3.832) *Uttamsa* and *avataṃsa* are both masculine; they denote an ear-ornament as well as a crest-jewel.
(3.3.833) *Vasu* refers to a class of deities, fire, a ray of light, a gem, and wealth.
(3.3.834) *Vedhāḥ* refers to Viṣṇu; as a feminine noun, it denotes a blessing (*āśis*), a well-wish, or the fang of a snake.
(3.3.835) *Lālasā* refers to longing or eagerness; it also denotes acts of violence such as theft and the like.
(3.3.836) *Prasūḥ* means a mare; furthermore, *rodasī* and *rodasī* denote the earth and the sky.
(3.3.837) *Jvālā* and *bhās* are feminine; *arci*, *jyotis*, *dyota*, and *dṛṣṭi* are not masculine.
(3.3.838) *Āgas* refers to sin or offense; *vayas* refers to a bird, youth, age, and so forth.
(3.3.839) *Varcas* refers to luster or excrement; *mahaḥ* refers to a festival or splendor.

(3.3.840) *Rajas* means quality (*guṇa*), the menses of a woman, Rāhu, and darkness; (3.3.841) *tamas* means quality and darkness; (3.3.841) *chandas* means meter and desire; (3.3.842) *tapas* means the practice of austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance; (3.3.842) *sahas* means strength, *sahā* means a path, and *nabhas*, *kham*, and *nabhās* mean the month of Śrāvaṇa.
(3.3.843) *okaḥ* means a dwelling, a home, or a refuge; *okas* means milk, and *payaḥ* means both milk and water.
(3.3.844) *ojas* means brilliance and strength; *srotas* means a sense organ and the current of a river.
(3.3.845) *Tejas* is used in the senses of majesty, brilliance, strength, and semen; it is also used as a tri-lingual [adjective] in these senses.
(3.3.846) *Vidvān* and *vidan* mean "learned"; *bībhatsaḥ* means "loathsome" or "cruel," and these may also be used in the sense of "excessive.
(3.3.847) *Jyāyān* is used for "old" and "praiseworthy"; *kanīyān*, however, is used for "young" and "small."
(3.3.848) *Varīyān* is used for *uru* and *vara*; *sādhīyān* for *sādhu* and *bāḍha*.
Thus end the words ending in *-ān*.
(3.3.849) *Barham* also means a leaf; *graha* refers to persistence, an eclipse, the sun, and so forth.
(3.3.850) *Niryūha* refers to a door-bolt, a decoction, and a turret;
(3.3.851) *Pragrāha* and *pragraha* refer to the string of a scale and the rein of a horse, etc.;
(3.3.852) *Parigraha* refers to a wife, attendants, property, roots, and curses.
(3.3.853) *Gṛha* means "wives" as well as "house"; *āroha* refers to the hips of an excellent woman.
(3.3.854) *Vyūha* means a "multitude" as well as [the serpent] Vṛtra; *agni*, *indu*, and *arka* mean those who dispel darkness.
(3.3.855) *Paribarha* refers to the equipment suitable for a king; the following words are indeclinables (*avyaya*).
Thus end those ending in *ha* (Pāṇini 1.4.49).

The particle *āṅ* is used in the sense of slightness, pervasion, and boundary when joined with a verbal root (1.4.50–52). The particle *ā* is optionally pragṛhya when used in recollection or in a sentence; it may also express anger or affliction.
(3.3.858) *pāpa*, *kutsā*, and *īṣadartha* [are the meanings of *ku*]; (3.3.859) *dhik* [is used] in reproach and censure;
(3.3.860) *ca* [is used] in conjunction, aggregation, and mutual collection;
*svasti* [is used] for benediction, welfare, merit, and the like; and *ati* [is used] for excellence and transgression.
(3.3.861) *Svit* is used in questioning and in deliberation; *tu* occurs in the sense of distinction and emphasis.
(3.3.862) *Sakṛt* means "together" or "at one time," while *ārāt* denotes both distance and proximity.
(3.3.863) *Paścāt* refers to the western direction and to what follows; *uta* is used for the senses of "also" and "option."

(3.3.864) *punar* is used in the sense of repetition and *saha*; (3.3.865) *śaśvat* and *sākṣāt* are used in the sense of "directly" and "manifestly"; (3.3.866) *bata* is used in expressions of weariness, compassion, contentment, wonder, and address; *hanta* is used in joy, compassion, the commencement of a sentence, and dejection.
(3.3.867) *prati* is used in the sense of a substitute (*pratinidhi*), distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth, according to usage;
(3.3.868) [it is used] in the senses of cause (*hetu*), section (*prakaraṇa*), excellence (*prakarṣa*), and completion (*samāpti*);
(3.3.869) *purastāt*, *prathamam*, and *purā* are also used in the sense of the eastern direction (*prācī*) and "in front" (*agrataḥ*).
(3.3.870) *yāvat* and *tāvat* [are used] in the senses of totality, limit, measure, and restriction;
(3.3.871) *atho* and *atha* [are used] in the senses of auspiciousness, immediate succession, commencement, inquiry, and entirety;
(3.3.872) *vṛthā* [is used] in the senses of being useless and non-prescriptive; *nānā* [is used] in the senses of manifoldness and both.

(3.3.873) *nu* [is used] in inquiry and in option; (3.3.874) *anu* [is used] in the sense of posteriority and similarity; (3.3.875) *nanu* [is used] in questioning, emphasis, permission, conciliation, and address;
it is also used in censure, conjunction, inquiry, doubt, and possibility.
(3.3.876) *Sāmi* is used in the sense of comparison or option; *tu* [is used] in the sense of "half" or when expressing contempt.
(3.3.877) *Amā* means "together with" (*saha*) or "nearby" (*samīpe*); *kaṃ* means "water" (*vāriṇi*) or "the head" (*mūrdhani*).
(3.3.878) *Iva* is used in the senses of "thus" (*ittham*) and "in this manner" (*evam*); *nūnam* is used in the sense of conjecture (*tarke*) or certainty regarding a matter (*arthaniścaye*).

(3.3.879) *joṣam* is used in the sense of silence and happiness; (3.3.880) *kim* is used in the sense of inquiry and loathing; (3.3.881) *nāma* is used in the senses of manifestation, possibility, anger, approach, and reproach; *alam* expresses ornament, sufficiency, capability, and prohibition.
(3.3.882) *huṃ* is used for deliberation (*vitarke*) and inquiry (*paripraśne*); *samayā* is used for proximity (*antikam*) and the middle (*madhye*).
(3.3.883) *punar* is used for repetition (*aprathe*) and division (*bhede*); *nir* is used for certainty (*niścaye*) and negation (*niṣedhe*).
(3.3.884) *purā* is used for continuity (*prabandhe*), the distant past (*cirātīte*), and the near future (*nikaṭāgāmike*).
(3.3.885) *ūrayi*, *ūrī*, and *corī*—these three are used for expansion and for acceptance.
(3.3.886) *Svar* is used for heaven and the other world; *kila* is used for report and the impossible.
(3.3.887) *Khalu* is used for prohibition, poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*), inquiry, and conciliation.
(3.3.888) *abhitaḥ* is used in the senses of proximity, on both sides, speed, entirety, and facing toward;
(3.3.889) *prāduḥ* is used in the senses of manifestation and name; *mithas* and *anyonyam* are used in the sense of secrecy as well;
(3.3.890) *tiras* is used in the sense of disappearance and in the sense of across; *hā* is used in the senses of despondency, grief, and departure.
(3.3.891) *Aha* is used in the sense of wonder and sorrow; *hi* is used in the sense of cause and restriction.
This concludes the section on words with multiple meanings (Section 3); herein are 256 root verses.
Kṣe.ślo. 24.
The Section on Indeclinables (Avyayavarga):
*cirāya*, *cirarātrāya*, *cirasya*, and others are words expressing duration (*cirārtha*).
*muhuḥ*, *punaḥ punaḥ*, *śaśvat*, *abhīkṣṇam*, and *asakṛt* are synonyms.
(3.4.894) *srāk*, *jhaṭiti*, *añjasā*, *ahnāya*, *drāk*, *maṅkṣu*, and *sapadi* denote speed;
(3.4.895) *balavat*, *suṣṭhu*, *kimuta*, *svati*, *atīva*, and [the particle] *ca* denote intensity;
(3.4.896) *pṛthak*, *vinā*, *antareṇa*, *ṛte*, *hiruk*, and *nānā* denote exclusion.
(3.4.897) *yat*, *tat*, *yatas*, and *tatas* [are used] in the sense of cause (*hetu*); (3.4.898) however, *cit*, *can*, and *cana* [are used] when the cause is not complete (*asākalya*).

(3.4.899) *kadācit*, *jātu*, *sārdham*, *sākam*, *satrā*, *samam*, and *saha* [are used in the sense of "together"]; *prādhvam* has the meaning of favorability (*ānukūlya*); whereas *vṛthā* and *mudhā* [are used] in the sense of being useless (*vyarthaka*).

(3.4.900) *āho*, *utāho*, *kimuta* are used in the sense of option (*vikalpa*); (3.4.901) *kiṃ*, *kimu*, *uta*; and (3.4.902) *tu*, *hi*, *ca*, *sma*, *ha*, *vai* are used for filling out a verse (*pādapūraṇa*), as well as for praise (*pūjana*) and intensity (*svati*); [furthermore,] *divā* and *ahnīti* [are used for day], while *doṣā* and *naktaṃ* are used for night (*rajanī*).

(3.4.903) *tiras* is used in the sense of "sideways" (*tiryag-artha*), and *tiro* is also [used in this sense]. Now, the following are used for the purpose of addressing (*saṃbodhana*): (3.4.904) *pyāṭ*, *pāṭ*, *aṅga*, *he*, *hai*, and *bhoḥ*. (3.4.905) *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *hiruk* [are used in the sense of proximity];
however, *sahasā* is used in the sense of "unexpectedly" (*atarkite*). *Puras*, *puratas*, and *agrataḥ* [are used in the sense of] "in front."

(3.4.906) *svāhā* is used for the offering of oblations to the gods; *śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *svadhā* [are likewise sacrificial interjections]. (3.4.907) *kiñcit*, *īṣat*, *manāk*, and *alpa* denote "slightly" or "a little. (3.4.908) *pretya* means "in another existence" or "hereafter"; *va*, *vā*, *yathā*, *tathā*, *eva*, and *evam* are used in the sense of "equality" or "likewise"; *aho* and *hī* are used in the sense of "wonder."
(3.4.909) *maunam* means silence; *tūṣṇīm*, *tūṣṇīkam*, *sadyas*, and *sapadi* mean at that very moment.
(3.4.910) *diṣṭyā* and *samupajoṣam* are used for joy; furthermore, *antare*, *antarā*, and *antareṇa* mean in the middle. (3.4.911) *prasahya* has the sense of force or compulsion.

(3.4.912) Two words are used for what is joined [to the present], namely *sāmpratam* and *sthāne*; *abhīkṣṇam*, *śaśvat*, and *anāratam* denote frequency. (3.4.913) *nahi*, *na*, *no*, *nāpi*, *mā sma*, and *mā* are used in the sense of negation; *alam* is used for prohibition.
(3.4.914) *cet* and *yadi* are used for an alternative view; *addhā* and *añjasā* are both used for truth.
(3.4.915) *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ* are used in the sense of manifestation; *om*, *evam*, and *paramam* are used in the sense of assent.
(3.4.916) *samantataḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *sarvataḥ*, and also *viṣvak* are used in the sense of "on all sides.
(3.4.917) *kāmaṃ* is used when giving consent to an unwilling person; *astu* is used in the sense of accepting with envy.
(3.4.918) Now, [the suffix *khal*] may occur after a word expressing contradiction; (3.4.919) it occurs after *kāma* in the sense of making one's desire known;

(3.4.920) *niṣṣama* and *duṣṣama* are used in the sense of censurable; *yathāsvam* and *yathāyatham* are used in their respective senses; *mṛṣā*, *mithyā*, and *vitatha* are used in the sense of falsehood; and *yathārtham* and *yathātatham* are used in the sense of truth.
(3.4.921) *syuḥ*, *eva*, *tu*, *punaḥ*, *vai*, and *vā* are words expressing restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
(3.4.922) *prāk* expresses a past sense; *nūnam* and *avaśyam*—these two—express certainty (*niścaya*).
(3.4.923) *saṃvat* refers to a year; *arvāk* and *avaras* mean "below" or "later"; *evam* means "thus," and *svayam* means "by oneself."
(3.4.924) *alpa* is used for "small," *nīcaiḥ* for "low," *mahat* for "great," *uccaiḥ* for "high"; *prāyaḥ* is used for "mostly" or "abundance," and *śanais* for "slowly" or "not quickly.
(3.4.925) *sanā* is used for "eternal," *bahiḥ* for "external," *smā* for "past," and *astam* for "disappearance.
(3.4.926) *asti* is used for "existence," *u* is used when speaking in anger, *ūm* in a question, and *tvayi* in conciliation.
(3.4.927) *huṃ* is used in reasoning; *uṣā* at the end of night; *namaḥ* in salutation. (3.4.928) *aṅga* in the sense of "again"; *duṣṭhu* in censure; *suṣṭhu* in praise.
(3.4.929) *sāyam* at evening; *prage* at dawn; *prātaḥ* at morning; *nikaṣā* in proximity.
(3.4.930) *amām* is used in the sense of non-conformity; *smaraṇe* (in remembrance); *huṃ* and *phaṭ* are used for the removal of obstacles.
(3.4.931) *arthe* (in the sense of "yes" or "so be it") is used in acceptance; *hūṃ* is used in calling out to one who is inferior; *hīn* is used in haste.
(3.4.932) *parut*, *parāri*, and *aiṣamaḥ* denote years; *pūrve* and *pūrvatare* denote past times. *yati* [is used as a technical term for a pause].

(3.4.933) [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *adya*, *atra*, and *ahni* to form *adyatanam*, *atrāhnam*, and *ahnaḥ* respectively. (3.4.934) Similarly, after *pūrva*, *uttara*, *apara*, *adhara*, *anya*, *anyatara*, and *itarata*, the suffixes [forming *pūrvāhṇa*, etc.,] are applied. (3.4.935) From these, *pūrvedyuḥ* and so forth are formed; likewise, *ubhayadyuḥ* and *ubhayedyuḥ* are formed, as well as *paretvahn* and *paredyavi*.
(3.4.936) *hyas* is used for the day gone by; *śvas* for the day not yet come; and *paraśvas* for the day after tomorrow.
(3.4.937) *tadā*, *tadānīm*, *yugapat*, *ekadā*, *sarvadā*, *sadā*. (3.4.938) *etarhi*, *saṃprati*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*, *sāmpratam*, and likewise *tathā*.
(3.4.939) Regarding direction, place, and time, beginning with "east" (*pūrva*), there are the forms *prāk*, *udak*, *pratyak*, and so forth.
This concludes the section on indeclinables (4), wherein the root verses number twenty-three.
The Section on the Compendium of Gender and Other Features.
Now begins the fifth section, the Compendium of Gender and Other Features (liṅgādisaṃgrahavarga).

[The gender and other features of words] are determined by the grammatical treatises on gender, as well as by those words derived from the *sann*-class suffixes, *kṛt* suffixes, *taddhita* suffixes, and compounds.

(3.5.941) Regarding things not explicitly mentioned, one should infer the gender here as if it were mixed. (3.5.942) The rule for the remainder of genders is pervasive, provided it is not sublated by specific exceptions. (3.5.943) Feminine endings are *ī*, *ū*, and monosyllabic words ending in a double consonant (*virāma*), as well as the names of female animals.
(3.5.944) The word *nāman* [is used] for lightning, night, creeper, lute, direction, earth, river, and modesty.
(3.5.945) A *dvigu* compound ending in a vowel other than *a* has a single meaning (*ekārtha*), except when it ends in *pātra*, *yuga*, and so forth.
(3.5.946) The suffix *tal* is applied in the sense of a collection (*vṛnda*); the suffixes *ya*, *nikaṭya*, *atra*, and *vairamaithunika* are derived with the suffix *vuñ*.

(3.5.947) After verbal roots meaning "to become female" and so forth, the suffixes *ani*, *ktin*, *ṇvul*, *ṇac*, *ṇvuc*, *kyap*, *yujiñ*, and *ṅniś* [are applied]. (3.5.948) Among the *uṇādi* suffixes, there are *nir* and *ūrī*; that which ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*), in *āṣ*, or in *ūḍ* is mobile or stable. (3.5.949) When it denotes a sport involving that [object], if it is a weapon, the suffix *ṇa* is applied, as in *mauṣṭa* ("boxing") and *pāllava* ("playing with twigs"); [the suffix] *dik* [is applied] in other cases.
(3.5.950) The suffix *ñ* replaces *ghañ*; if that action occurs on this [day], it is called *dāṇḍapātā* when it is the month of Phālguna.
(3.5.951) Likewise, *śyainampātā* refers to hunting, and *tailampātā* to the *svadhā* offering; such is the direction [of the rule].
(3.5.952) If there is a desire to express diminution, a feminine form such as *mṛṇālī* and so forth may be used.

(3.5.953) *laṅkā*, *śephālikā*, *ṭīkā*, *dhātakī*, *pañcikā*, *āḍhakī*; (3.5.954) *sidhrakā*, *sārikā*, *hikkā*, *prācikā*, *ulkā*, *pipīlikā*; (3.5.955) *tindukī*, *kaṇikā*, *bhaṅgiḥ*, *suraṅga*, *sūci*, *māḍhyaḥ*.
(3.5.956) *Picchā*, *vitaṇḍā*, *kākiṇī*, *cūrṇiḥ*, *śāṇī*, *druṇī*, *darat*;
(3.5.957) *sātiḥ*, *kanthā*, likewise *āsandī*, *nābhī*, and also *rājasabhā*; (3.5.958) *jhallarī*, *carcarī*, *pārī*, *horā*, *laṭvā*, and *sidhmalā*.
(3.5.959) *lākṣā*, *likṣā*, *gaṇḍūṣā*, *gṛdhrasī*, *camasī*, and *masī*—
this is the summary of feminine gender terms.
(3.5.960) In the masculine gender, the gods (*sura*) and demons (*asura*), along with their various divisions and attendants, are included together with their synonyms.
(3.5.961) Heaven, sacrifice, mountain, cloud, ocean, tree, time, sword, arrow, and enemy;
(3.5.962) hand, cheek, lip, arm, tooth, throat, hair, nail, and breast;
(3.5.963) words ending in *ahna* and *aha*, varieties of battle cries, and words ending in *rātri* when preceded by a numeral other than one.

(3.5.964) Resins such as *śrīveṣṭa* and others ending in the suffix *-as* are [masculine], provided they are not otherwise contradicted [by other rules]. (3.5.965) With the exception of *kaśeru*, *jatu*, and *vastu*, those ending in *tu* or *ru* have a virāma [after the penultimate vowel]. (3.5.966) Furthermore, if these words ending in *y* or *d* have *kaṣaṇa*, *bha*, or *mara* as their penultimate syllables, [they are masculine].
(3.5.967) Words denoting lineages (*gotra*) ending in *pathin*, *nayana*, and *saṭa*, as well as those called Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), [are masculine].

(3.5.968) The suffixes *ghañ*, *jab*, *naṅ*, *ṇa*, *gha*, and *āthuc* occur after verbal roots when forming names (*nāman*) or when expressing the action itself (*bhāva*), provided they do not denote the agent (*akarta*).

(3.5.969) The suffix *lyu* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); the suffix *iman* occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāva*); the suffix *ka* occurs after a root ending in *ghu*; and the suffix *ki* occurs after a root beginning with *pra* and others.

(3.5.970) In a *dvandva* compound, the forms *aśvavaḍavau* and *aśvavaḍavā* are used when not denoting a collective; (3.5.971) the word *kāntaḥ* is used when preceded by synonyms of the sun or the moon, as well as when preceded by *ayaḥ*; (3.5.972) and likewise [the suffix *kan* is applied] to *vaṭakaḥ*, *anuvākaḥ*, *rallakaḥ*, and *kuḍaṅgakaḥ*.

(3.5.973) *puṅkha*, *nyūṅkha*, and *samudra*; *viṭapa*, *ṭaṭa*, *dhaṭa*, and *khaṭā*; (3.5.974) *koṭṭa*, *araghaṭṭa*, and *haṭṭa*; as well as *piṇḍa*, *goṇḍa*, and *picaṇḍa*; (3.5.975) *gaḍu*, *karaṇḍa*, *laguḍa*, *karaṇḍa* [again], *kiṇa*, and *ghuṇa*.
(3.5.976) *dṛti*, *sīmanta*, *harita*, *romantha*, *udgītha*, and *budbuda*;
(3.5.977) *kāsamarda*, *arbuda*, *kunda*, *phena*, *stūpa*, and *yūpaka*;
(3.5.978) *ātapa*, *nābhi*, *kuṇapa*, *kṣura*, and *kedara* [are used as masculine when referring to a Kṣatriya].
(3.5.979) *pūr*, *kṣurapr*, and *cukra*; and *gol*, *hiṅgula*, and *pudgala*.
(3.5.980) *vetāla*, *bhall*, *malla*, and *purāḍāśa*; also *paṭṭiśa*.
(3.5.981) *kulmāṣa*, *rabhasa*, *kaṭāha*, and *patadraha*.

Thus concludes the summary of masculine remainders (3.5.982). Furthermore, in the case of a pair [of opposites], other [terms] are also [masculine]: *khāraṇya*, *parṇaśvabhra*, *himodaka*, *śītoṣṇa*, *māṃsarudhira*, *mukhākṣi*, and *draviṇabala*. (3.5.983)
(3.5.984) *phala*, *hema*, *śulba*, *loha*, *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *śubha*, *aśubha*;
(3.5.985) *jalapuṣpa* (aquatic flowers), *lavaṇa* (salt), *vyañjana* (condiments/sides), *anulepana* (unguents);
(3.5.986) numbers such as *koṭi*, *śata*, and so forth, as well as *lakṣa* and *niyuta*.

(3.5.987) A *dvigu* compound ending in *dvi*, *aṣṭan*, *as*, *su*, or *san*, provided it does not end in *ā* and does not denote an agent; (3.5.988) a word ending in *trā* with a *s* as its penultimate letter, provided it is taught [by Pāṇini] and ends in *rātra* preceded by a numeral;
(3.5.989) a *dvigu* compound whose final member is *pātra* or another word ending in *yat* has a single meaning, according to the usage of the examples.

(3.5.990) A *dvandva* compound denoting singularity and an *avyayībhāva* compound [ending in -pathin] take the suffix *aC* when following a numeral or an indeclinable. (3.5.991) After the word *ṣaḍi*, the suffix *aC* is applied to *chāyā* when it denotes many things; [the suffix *aC* is applied to *chāyā*] to form *vicchāyam*. (3.5.992) The suffix *aC* is applied to *sabhā* when it denotes a collection, even if it ends in *śālā*; provided that it follows a word meaning "king" or "non-human," except for words meaning "kingless."
(3.5.993) *dāsīsabhaṃ*, *nṛpasabhaṃ*, *rakṣassabham*—these [words] denote directions.

(3.5.994) A word ending in *upajñā* or *upakrama* is used to indicate that [the work] began with that person. (3.5.995) [The suffix] *ka* is added after *upajñā* and *upakrama* when they refer to the names of [people from] Kantha and Uśīnara respectively.

(3.5.996) In the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), suffixes other than *na*, *ṇa*, and *kvip* are applied; in the sense of a collection (*samūha*), they are applied to express both the abstract state and the object (*karma*).
(3.5.997) Suffixes ending in *a* are applied after the words *puṇya* and *sudinī*, when followed by the word *ahar*.
(3.5.998) Distinctive qualifiers of actions and indeclinables, even when [the action] is singular, take the suffix *uktha* and *toṭaka*.
(3.5.999) *coca*, *piccha*, *gṛhasthūṇa*, *tirīṭa*, *marma*, *yojana*;
(3.5.1000) *rājasūya*, *vājapeya*, and the prose and verse (*gadyapadye*) composed by a poet;
(3.5.1001) *māṇikya*, *bhāṣya*, *sindūra*, *cīra*, *cīvara*, and *piñjara*.
(3.5.1002) *Lokāyata*, *haritāla*, *vidala*, *sthāla*, and *bāhlika*—
this is the summary of the section on neuter remainders. (3.5.1003) Among masculine and neuter nouns, the remainder consists of *ardharca*, *piṇyāka*, and *kaṇṭaka*.
(3.5.1004) Modaka, taṇḍaka, ṭaṅka, śāṭaka, karpaṭa, arbuda; (3.5.1005) pātaka, udyoga, caraka, tamāla, āmalaka, naḍa;
(3.5.1006) kuṣṭha, muṇḍa, śīdhu, busta, kṣveḍita, kṣema, kuṭṭima.
(3.5.1007) *saṃgama*, *śatamāna*, *arma*, *śambala*, *avyaya*, *tāṇḍava*;
(3.5.1008) *kaviya*, *kanda*, *kārpāsa*, *pārāvāra*, *yugandhara*; (3.5.1009) *yūpa*, *pragrīva*, *pātrīva*, *yūṣa*, *camasa*, *cikkasa*.

(3.5.1010) In the *ardharca* group and others, the masculine gender and so forth of words such as *ghṛta* are fixed by Vedic usage. (3.5.1011) Therefore, that [usage] is not mentioned here; yet if it exists even in this world, let it be, as in the case of the remainder (*śeṣa*).
Thus concludes the summary of the remainder consisting of masculine and neuter genders.
(3.5.1012) The offspring of male and female [beings] ending in [the suffixes] -a, -i, -u, and -ṛ;

(3.5.1013) the various species of animals, those with masculine names, and [names] joined with feminine [suffixes], such as *mallaka*; (3.5.1014) *ūrmi*, *varāṭaka*, *svāti*, *varṇaka*, *jhāṭali*, and *manu*.
(3.5.1015) *mūṣā*, *sṛpāṭī*, *karkandhūḥ*, *yaṣṭiḥ*, *śāṭī*, *kaṭī*, *kuṭī*—

this is the compendium of words that remain [unchanged] as both feminine and masculine. (3.5.1016) The suffix *vyañ* occurs after verbal roots to denote abstract state (*bhāva*) and action (*kriyā*), and in some cases, the suffix *vuñ* also occurs.
(3.5.1017) From *aucitya* and *aucitī*, [the suffix] *maitrī* and *maitrya*; *vuñ* has been illustrated previously.
(3.5.1018) When preceded by a word ending in the genitive case, the words *senā*, *chāyā*, *śālā*, *surā*, and *niśā* [take the suffix *ṭac*].
(3.5.1019) It may optionally be *nṛsenaṃ* or *śvaniśaṃ*; for others, the direction is otherwise.
(3.5.1020) A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in a long vowel (*ābannanta*) is feminine; (3.5.1021) and for such a *dvigu*, the neuter suffix *naṅ* is also elided (*lup*).
Thus: *trikhaṭvam* and *trikhaṭvī*, as well as *tritakṣam* and *tritakṣī*.
This concludes the summary of the remaining feminine and neuter forms.
(3.5.1022) *pātrī*, *puṭī*, *vāṭī*, *peṭī*, *kuvala*, and *dāḍima* [are feminine];

(3.5.1023) thus ends the summary of the remaining [words] with three genders; (3.5.1024) in a *dvandva* compound where its own members are predominant, as well as in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the gender of the final member prevails.
(3.5.1025) Words beginning with *pra* and ending in *artha*, as well as *alaṃ*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna*, when preceded by another word, [form a compound].

(3.5.1026) A *dvigu* compound, which expresses the meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), consists of a numeral followed by a noun that ends in a universal term (*sarvanāman*) or another numeral. (3.5.1027) A *bahuvrīhi* compound [is formed] with words other than those denoting directions; its examples should be inferred accordingly.
(3.5.1028) Qualities, substances, actions, and conjunctions are adjuncts that transfer to another.

(3.5.1029) Kṛt suffixes, except for those used as technical names, [denote] the agent; kṛtya suffixes denote the agent or the object. (3.5.1030) Suffixes beginning with *aṇ* and others, when applied in senses such as "colored by that," serve to distinguish various meanings.

(3.5.1031) Those termed *ṣat* are the same in all three genders; (3.5.1032) *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, verbal endings (*tiṅ*), and indeclinables [are also the same]. In case of conflict, the latter [prevails]; the remainder, however, should be understood from the usage of the learned.
Thus ends the fifth section, the "Compendium on Gender and so forth."

thus, in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* composed by Amarasimha,
the third section, the General Section (*sāmānyakāṇḍa*), has been fully established along with its supplements.
Thus ends the third section on general subjects;
thus the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* composed by Amarasiṃha, consisting of three sections and complete with its primary and secondary parts, has reached its conclusion.
